title: EV Fires Behave Like Conventional Car Fires
content:
Battery News
Automotive & Mobility
Testing & Safety
New research from UL finds electric vehicle fires behave much like conventional car fires, contrary to widespread assumptions about intensity.
August 5, 2026
4 Min Read
Carmakers can give firefighters a better chance to extinguish EV battery fires with possible adjustments to battery pack design.
Witthay Prasongsin via Getty Images
At a Glance
Battery access for firefighters remains a key challenge despite similar fire behavior.
Thermal runaway timing varies widely between EV models, affecting fire growth rates.
Standardizing emergency features across EV brands could improve responder safety.
EV battery fires
are an issue that looms large in the popular imagination, but they are poorly understood and documented. Indeed, a 2025
U.S. Fire Administration report on EV fires
says in its introduction, “There are substantial gaps in the science available to inform safe and effective approaches for identifying, confining, and extinguishing EV fires.
The report identified these three current challenges:
Limited science-based guidance for fire departments, EMS, law enforcement, towing operators, and the automotive recovery industry.
Significant differences in battery types, chemistry, location, and size across different EV brands, models, and years.
Existing tactics, tools, and procedures for addressing EV fires are not always based on scientific evidence.
With this in mind,
UL Research Institutes’ Fire Safety Research Institute
undertook a
project to document the nature of EV fires
and came to the somewhat surprising conclusion that EVs burn similarly to combustion-powered vehicles. Conventional wisdom has been that, while EVs catch fire less frequently than ICE cars, their fires burn with greater intensity.
UL Research Institutes initiated battery fires in EVs and found that “fire dynamics and associated chemical hazard in both EVs and ICEVs are primarily driven by the fire in the passenger compartment materials, and thus were similar between powertrain types.”
That means that the technical details of both kinds of fires are more similar than was expected. “The time to burnout, peak heat release rate, and total energy release were similar between EVs and ICEVs,” the report states. “Though anecdotally there have been concerns about major differences in EV fire behavior, no evidence was found that EVs burn hotter, or last longer than their conventional counterparts.”
The EVs in the test showed more variability in the fire growth rate than the ICE vehicles, with some growing faster and others more slowly than the conventional vehicles that were set on fire. Video analysis of the fires revealed that this is because of the time between the first recognition of a thermal runaway in the battery pack and the time needed for visible flames to emerge that then set the rest of the car alight.
"This research provides the fire service with evidence-based tactics they can implement immediately to improve firefighter safety and operations during EV fire incidents,” said
Adam Barowy
, Principal Research Engineer, UL Research Institutes, Fire Safety Research Institute. “By understanding fire behavior, exposure hazards, and the effectiveness of standard suppression strategies, fire departments can make informed tactical decisions that protect their teams and the communities they serve."
While the research was intended for firefighters, carmakers can also benefit as they consider design options when developing future EVs. “Overcoming the challenges associated with EV fire suppression will likely require continued advances in battery and vehicle safety engineering alongside improvements in firefighting tools and tactics,” the report acknowledged.
One of the toughest challenges that firefighters faced when battling the EV fires was getting enough cooling water to the battery cells that were undergoing thermal runaway. Carmakers go to great lengths to protect the battery cells from outside intrusion in the event of a crash, but this complicates firefighting. “Designs which facilitate better firefighter access to the battery during rare but severe fire events may warrant further consideration,” the report found.
Researchers cited the example of the Renault Zoe, a car that includes a firefighter access port in the battery case that allows water to be sprayed inside the battery enclosure. They acknowledge the potential for unintended side effects of such a feature, such as the potential for it to become a pathway for battery effluent to enter the passenger compartment, increasing the risk of explosion.
The UL researchers also point to the value of standardization of emergency responder-facing features, such as high-voltage disconnects, vent locations, and safety markings. This would simplify emergency operations for responders who wouldn’t have to consider as much variety among manufacturers.
The discontinued Renault Zoe EV's battery pack featured a port for firefighters to introduce water in case of a fire. RENAULT
Carmakers endeavor to ensure sufficient cooling for the cells in a pack to preserve their longevity and performance, and also to reduce the potential for thermal runaway. But, once runaway starts, variations in battery pack construction appear to make no difference in its propagation, according to the UL team.
However, researchers don’t rule out the potential for continued progress in this area. “Advances in battery cells, chemistries, and pack designs that improve resistance to thermal runaway propagation, while balancing the many competing objectives of vehicle design, could reduce the resources required for fire suppression and improve responder safety,” the report states, perhaps optimistically. “Ongoing collaboration and open communication between vehicle manufacturers, battery developers, researchers, and the fire service will likely be important in achieving these goals.”
Certainly, this seems like a worthy objective and ample motivation for all four groups to pursue improvements in this area.

title: CATL achieves sodium-ion battery mass production
content:
Design & Manufacturing
Battery Applications
CATL's Naxtra sodium-ion battery reaches GWh-scale mass production while a 60 GWh supply agreement with HyperStrong marks the largest sodium-ion deal recorded to date.
August 5, 2026
4 Min Read
CATL's Chief Scientist Dr. Wu Kai at the company's Technology Day event in Beijing on April 21, 2026.
At a Glance
CATL signed a 60 GWh sodium-ion supply agreement with energy storage integrator HyperStrong in China
The Naxtra sodium-ion battery achieved GWh-scale industrialization with full production starting in 2026
Sodium-ion cells use no cobalt or lithium and employ aluminum collectors on both electrodes for cost cuts
For years, sodium-ion batteries were considered a chemistry with compelling structural advantages, but that couldnt reach commercial relevance.
Benefiting from sodium’s abundance, an architecture that omits lithium and cobalt, and lower cell expansion stress, the chemistry has many promising features that exceed lithium-ion batteries. However, manufacturing reality tells a different story. Hard carbon anode production is difficult to control at volume, moisture sensitivity introduces yield problems, and the industry lacks the supply chain depth to support GWh-scale deployment with any consistency.
Now, that picture is starting to change.
In this article, we'll take a look at CATL's recent sodium-ion milestones, including a
landmark 60 GWh supply agreement
with energy storage integrator HyperStrong and the
formal announcement
of GWh-scale industrialization of the Naxtra Sodium-ion Battery.
Sodium-ion vs. lithium-ion batteries
Sodium-ion cells follow the same intercalation principle as lithium-ion, with ions moving between the cathode and anode during charge and discharge. However, sodium-ion’s design makes it significantly cheaper than lithium-ion.
Related:
How Battery Validation is Shaping the Future Grid
First, sodium is far more abundant than lithium, and sodium-ion cells use no cobalt. In addition, sodium-ion cells can use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, eliminating the copper required on lithium-ion anodes. With these material characteristics combined, sodium-ion batteries carry a low cost that suits large-scale, long-duration stationary storage, where raw material cost influences project budgets.
Meanwhile, sodium-ion batteries offer a slew of performance and reliability benefits as well. According to the
American Physical Society
, sodium-ion cells tolerate wider temperature ranges than conventional lithium-ion chemistries, maintain cycle stability at high ambient temperatures, and generate less heat during operation, reducing the burden on thermal management systems.
Where sodium-ion falls short is energy density and ease of manufacturing. Sodium-ion cells store less energy per kilogram than LFP (lithium iron phosphate), and their hard carbon anodes are more difficult to produce consistently as compared to graphite anodes used in lithium-ion designs. Controlling gas generation in hard carbon production, managing moisture exposure, achieving reliable adhesion of the aluminum current collector, and tuning anode formation protocols are only some of the engineering obstacles that have kept sodium-ion batteries from volume production.
Related:
Startups Pitch Investors to Transform the Battery Industry
CATL and HyperStrong’s 60-GWh sodium-ion agreement
In April of this year, CATL and energy storage integrator HyperStrong
signed a strategic cooperation agreement
in Ningde, China, covering a three-year, 60 GWh sodium-ion battery supply commitment. CATL describes the agreement as the largest sodium-ion battery supply deal in the world to date, and HyperStrong as the company's first strategic partner for sodium-ion energy storage. Their collaboration covers technology research and development, product applications, and project deployment.
CATL and HyperStrong representatives at the signing ceremony. Credit: CATL
CATL and HyperStrong representatives at the signing ceremony. Credit:
The agreement rests on manufacturing capabilities that CATL claims to have developed across the full sodium-ion production process. For example, the company claims notable energy density gains compared to previous commercial sodium-ion attempts, owing to a combination of morphology control and surface modification. On the production side, CATL says it resolved key process challenges by applying angstrom-level pore size regulation, surface molecular water-locking, and adaptive dynamic formation, each aimed at ensuring output consistency at high volumes.
CATL also notes that its sodium-ion cells share a platform-based design with the same form factor as its lithium-ion products. According to the company, that design choice reduces integration costs for operators and shortens the time from product qualification to power station deployment.
Related:
Breaking Down the Limits of Solid-State Battery Performance
CATL’s Naxtra Battery Reaches GWh-Scale Production
Meanwhile, at CATL's Super Technology Day in Beijing this year, the company
announced
that its Naxtra sodium-ion battery has achieved GWh-level industrialization. CATL describes the Naxtra as the result of systematically resolving hundreds of engineering challenges, with particular focus on four bottlenecks it identified as blocking sodium-ion mass production:
Extreme water control
Gas generation in hard carbon production lines
Aluminum foil adhesion
Self-forming anode systems
CATL says full-scale mass production will begin by the end of 2026.
The Naxtra sodium-ion battery marks CATL’s transition from the lab to gigawatt-hour scale manufacturing of sodium-ion technology. Credit: CATL
The Naxtra sodium-ion battery marks CATL’s transition from the lab to gigawatt-hour scale manufacturing of sodium-ion technology. Credit:
Taken together, the HyperStrong agreement and the Naxtra industrialization announcement show CATL’s involvement in two sides of the push for sodium-ion adoption. One demonstrates the chemistry’s commercial demand at scale, while the other shows that they can deliver the manufacturing capacity to meet it.
The open question now is whether hard carbon anode supply chains can develop at the pace that matches CATL’s commitments and timelines. The answer to that question will dictate the scale to which CATL and other battery manufacturers can produce sodium-ion cells.

title: EQONIC Advances Aluminum Battery Technology for Sustainability
content:
Battery Manufacturing
Materials
Design & Manufacturing
Industry Outlook
EQONIC introduces aluminum battery technology focused on affordability, sustainability, and scalability, addressing key challenges in energy storage solutions.
August 5, 2026
3 Min Read
Eqonic confirmed its proprietary, lithium-free composite has aluminum as its core material.
Eqonic Group.
EQONIC Group—a UK-based battery technology startup—has announced aluminum as the core material in its new lithium-free, sodium-free, and rare-earth-free battery technology. This development marks a great step toward a cost-effective and sustainable alternative to traditional battery chemistries such as
lithium-ion batteries
. The company is now moving to the next step, industrial validation, a critical phase in preparing the technology for commercial deployment.
Driving cost efficiency
According to the company, its aluminum-based battery technology has the potential to significantly reduce costs.
has set a target manufactured cost of £50/kWh at scale, which is approximately half the industry average for lithium-ion batteries. This cost reduction could make battery energy storage systems (BESS) and electric vehicles (EVs) more affordable, potentially accelerating the adoption of renewable energy technologies.
Related:
Driving Innovation in Europe Battery Manufacturing with CATL
“Aluminum-based chemistry gives us everything we set out to achieve – material abundance, high levels of safety, and low cost – without the trade-offs that lithium, sodium, and rare earth materials carry,” stated Jas Kandola, Founder and CEO of EQONIC Group. By focusing on affordability, EQONIC aims to address one of the key barriers to widespread adoption of energy storage solutions.
Sustainability through abundant materials
Aluminum, one of the most abundant elements on Earth, offers a sustainable and widely available alternative to materials like
lithium and other critical minerals
, which are often associated with supply chain challenges and environmental concerns. EQONIC’s choice of aluminum aligns with its goal of creating a more sustainable battery technology while ensuring a stable and cost-effective supply chain.
The company’s decision to avoid sodium, another emerging chemistry in battery technology, is notable. According to
, while sodium-ion battery adoption is growing, especially in BESS applications, these batteries still face challenges with scalability and supply chain efficiency. By focusing on aluminum, EQONIC aims to bypass these challenges entirely, leveraging a material that is not only abundant but also supported by well-established, responsibly managed supply chains. This focus on sustainability could make EQONIC’s technology an attractive option for industries seeking to reduce their environmental impact while maintaining cost efficiency.
EQONIC confirms aluminum as the chemistry behind its breakthrough battery technology. Courtesy of Eqonic.
Progressing toward industrial validation
EQONIC is now advancing its aluminum-based technology toward industrial validation, a critical step in transitioning from laboratory research to commercial readiness. This phase will involve rigorous testing to assess the manufacturability, performance, and reliability of the technology at scale.
Related:
Building the Future of Battery Technology in Upstate New York
“Confirming the chemistry is one part of the story; progressing towards industrial validation is the part that matters most, and that’s exactly where our focus is now,” Kandola stated. Industrial validation is essential for ensuring that the technology can meet the demands of real-world applications and achieve the reliability required for widespread adoption.
The next steps in EQONIC’s journey will be critical. Industrial validation will play a pivotal role in demonstrating the technology’s performance and reliability, ensuring it is ready for commercial deployment. As the company continues to progress, its focus on cost efficiency and sustainability positions it as a noteworthy player in the evolving energy storage landscape. The use of abundant materials like aluminum, combined with third-party validation, will be essential in building trust and ensuring the long-term viability of this new lithium-free battery technology.
About the Author
Maria Guerra
Senior Editor-Battery Technology, Informa Markets
Maria L. Guerra is a Senior Editor at
Battery Technology
, blending her engineering background with a passion for technology journalism. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Universidad Metropolitana in Caracas, Venezuela, and a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering.
Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. During her internship at Pequiven S.A. in Venezuela, she trained neural networks using MATLAB (Kohonen Map) to estimate electrical circuit variables for oil wells (e.g., voltage, current, and power).
In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at

title: RapidRatings: Turning Supply Chain Risk Into Resilience
content:
RapidRatings: Turning Supply Chain Risk Into Resilience
Prioritise Us
on Google
Watch this on-demand webinar to hear how leading organisations are turning turbulence into resilience. Credit: Getty
Watch an on-demand webinar to gain insights from Tom Derry and James Gellert about how leading companies are navigating ongoing supply chain risk
Supply chain turbulence has been rife in recent years, driven by changing legislation and rising volatility. Tom Derry, former CEO of ISM and James Gellert, Executive Chair of
RapidRatings
, know this risk all too well.
In an on-demand webinar, Tom and James explore how teams navigate constant disruption, financial vulnerability and the collapse of globalisation's consensus in modern supply networks.
Their discussion examines how procurement organisations navigate an environment where disruption has become normal rather than exceptional.
now on-demand.
Evolution of globalisation assumptions
Tom became CEO of ISM in 2012. According to Tom, the organisation operated under assumptions that had existed for nearly 20 years, from the mid nineties to the mid 2010s.
"I use Brexit as my milestone event, because it signalled that the consensus around the benefits of globalisation and open country markets was beginning to fragment — that there were risks associated with it," says Tom.
Tom Derry, former CEO of ISM (Credit: ISM)
Over the next decade, ISM witnessed the unravelling of the globalisation consensus. The COVID-19 pandemic followed, then a series of geopolitical tensions that did not exist before.
James brings expertise from corporate finance and risk. Before RapidRatings, he built and ran three companies in data, analytics and technology, having started as a banker focused on credit and fixed income.
RapidRatings works with clients across roughly 27 industries. The company exposes financial
vulnerabilities
hiding within supply networks that rarely appear until it is too late, and that link directly to operational and reputational risks procurement teams are judged on.
RapidRatings 2025 findings:
85% of enterprises experienced increased costs
42% experienced production disruptions due to supply chain issues, and a quarter experienced quality issues
81% of enterprises experienced disruptions of one kind or another in their supply chain, yet their suppliers themselves reported a lower rate of impact
Decision making in permacrisis
Supply chain and procurement teams are responding to challenges that arrive faster and with greater impact than before.
According to James
, much of what the industry faces today ties back to the concept of permacrisis.
Factors include the interest rate environment, the macroeconomic environment, managing working capital, private credit, private equity, the capital markets and geopolitical and economic risks.
"It used to be the case that you were doing your job well if product showed up on time and in full. That's how performance was measured. That began to change during the pandemic, and it's certainly the case today," says Tom.
"It's no longer enough to say your product arrived on time and the quality was good. These existential factors for the company are now being evaluated, and you're being evaluated on them. That's a real change."
Performance measurement has expanded beyond traditional delivery metrics. Procurement professionals now face accountability for factors that affect company survival.
Financial health as predictor
Financial health is a foundational indicator of how well positioned a company is to meet its obligations. Historically, many businesses and supply chain organisations have worked in silos, with different people looking at financial risk,
cybersecurity risk
, ESG and governance factors, and more traditional measures like quality and delivery.
"Ultimately, though, a company's financial health is a leading indicator of whether it can meet all of those other obligations, or whether it's presenting new risks in those areas that it wasn't before," says James.
There's been a change in the fundamental way of thinking — not just in the United States, but around the world — and in the policies countries are using to gain advantage in the global commercial game.
Watch On-Demand
James describes a K-shaped economy pattern in the corporate world. Companies doing well tend to be the larger, public ones. Companies doing less well tend to be middle market and private, because they act as the shock absorbers for supply chains.
"If I were in the audience thinking about my own supply base, my first instinct might be to assume it isn't in that kind of distress. I'd challenge that assumption — there are undoubtedly examples in your supply base; you just need to go and find them, and ask the tough questions if you haven't already," says Tom.
Tom compares the situation to an individual living paycheque to paycheque, making only minimum payments on credit cards without reducing actual debt. "That's not sustainable for me as an individual, and it's equally true for companies. I think we underestimate how much
stress exists in the supply base
Criticality beyond spend levels
A common mistake in supply chain risk management is ignoring apparently low levels of spend. Tom gives an example of a pharmaceutical company where the coating on a tablet represented an inconsequential level of spend for the company, but it supported US$2bn in revenue.
James Gellert, Executive Chair of RapidRatings (Credit: BizClik Media)
"Without that coating, they couldn't sell the product. So don't segment purely by level of spend — think about risk in terms of how much revenue and sales a given supplier supports, and
assess your risk
According to James, criticality is not the same as spend. Criticality can be measured in different ways.
"For me, the most important thing organisations can do is share information across risk domains and mandate that coordination, because a problem in financial health is often a leading indicator of problems elsewhere. You can't work in silos anymore," James adds.
The conversation between Tom and James is available to watch on demand. Their combined experience in procurement policy and corporate finance could provide insight for organisations navigating instability in supplier networks.

title: Jim Bureau: Building Resilience Amid Ongoing Climate Risk
content:
Jim Bureau: Building Resilience Amid Ongoing Climate Risk
Prioritise Us
on Google
Jim Bureau, CEO of Loftware, talks to Supply Chain Digital about the supply chain risk of El Niño. Credit: Loftware
In a time defined by ongoing extreme climate events, Jim Bureau, CEO of Loftware, explores how businesses are responding to growing geopolitical disruption
In recent years, major climate events have become more and more regular, causing disruption to supply chain operations around the world. Inconsistencies with rainfall and drought have caused crops, including cocoa beans, coffee beans and
– the leaves behind matcha – to fail.
Now, extreme and unseasonable temperatures have sparked wildfires around the world. Events which were once a disruptive but rare occurrence have now become a common feat. As a result, organisations around the world are having to learn how operate alongside them, instead of reacting to them.
Loftware helps more than 16,000 organisations manage supply chain risk amid ongoing complexity, through its improved collaboration and visibility. Loftware's solutions provide greater agility to changing conditions and significant aid with compliance.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Jim Bureau, the CEO of Loftware, about ongoing climate events could become the latest global supply chain shock, disrupting trade flows, business operations and
food production
How has extreme weather impacted global supply chains?
Extreme weather has become
more than a seasonal disruption
; it's changing how supply chains operate. Recent heatwaves across Europe affected transport networks, inland shipping, energy infrastructure, agricultural production and labour availability simultaneously. Because today's supply chains are highly interconnected, disruption in one region quickly creates knock-on effects across manufacturing, logistics, inventory and customer fulfilment around the world.
The assumption can no longer be that disruption is temporary. Businesses need to plan for volatility as a constant rather than the exception.
How are climate events forcing businesses around the world to rethink their sourcing strategies and supplier diversification?
Many organisations are moving away from relying heavily on a single supplier, region or transport route. Diversification is becoming essential, but adding suppliers also adds complexity.
The challenge isn't simply finding alternative sources. It's ensuring every supplier, manufacturer and logistics partner has access to accurate product information, labelling requirements and compliance data. Without that
shared visibility
, diversification can introduce as much risk as it removes.
Heatwaves across Europe have led to major wildfires. Credit: Getty Images
How is disruption at shipping and trade chokepoints impacting global supply chains?
Whether it's low river levels restricting inland shipping, ports operating below capacity or delays at major trade routes, chokepoints create ripple effects throughout the supply chain. Companies often have to reroute shipments, change production schedules or source products differently at short notice.
The organisations that respond most effectively are those that can make informed decisions quickly because they have real-time connected data and close collaboration across their entire supply chain network.
What can organisations do to ensure they remain operable amid disruption and last-minute changes?
Resilience today depends less on having
bigger stockpiles
and more on having better information. Businesses need real-time visibility across suppliers, manufacturing sites, logistics providers and customers so they can respond quickly without sacrificing compliance or accuracy.
But visibility alone isn't enough. Organisations also need the ability to execute changes consistently across their entire supply chain. When production shifts to a new facility, an alternative supplier is onboarded or products are redirected to a different market, every label, packaging specification, language requirement and regulatory declaration needs to be updated accurately and immediately.
That's why product identification has become a strategic capability rather than an operational afterthought. Companies that centralise and standardise product identification while enabling secure collaboration across trading partners can adapt far more quickly, reduce the risk of errors and keep products moving, even as conditions change around them.
Digital platforms can help increase visibility and resilience. Credit: Getty Images
What can supply chains learn about resilience following ongoing disruption?
The biggest lesson is that resilience is no longer about recovering after disruption; it's about operating effectively despite it.
That requires stronger collaboration across the supply chain, trusted product data and digital platforms that allow organisations to coordinate decisions in real time.
Climate events
, geopolitical uncertainty and regulatory change are all increasing pressure on global operations, but businesses that build better connected supply chain ecosystems will be far better positioned to adapt.
Ultimately, resilience isn't measured by how rarely disruption occurs. It's measured by how confidently an organisation can respond when it does.

title: Nissin Foods Turns to Blue Yonder for Smarter Supply Chains
content:
Nissin Foods Turns to Blue Yonder for Smarter Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Nissin Foods has partnered with Blue Yonder and Highspring to transform its supply chain planning. Credit: Nissin Foods
Nissin Foods is digitising its supply chain planning amid ongoing market volatility, turning towards expertise from Blue Yonder and Highspring
Nissin Foods USA has announced its partnership with
Blue Yonder
and Highspring in order to undertake a digital transformation.
The company is overhauling its supply chain management, moving away from legacy tools and towards greater integration and flexibility.
Through this, Nissin will be able to respond better to changing demand, improve product availability and reduce costs.
Navigating complexity
In today's world, supply chains operating on manual spreadsheets and legacy systems are susceptible to risk. Across the industry, companies are facing ongoing supply chain challenges, with talent shortages, ageing workforces and rising operational complexity.
To mitigate the fallout, Nissin Foods is turning to Blue Yonder and Highspring to transform its demand and supply planning capabilities. title: Watch Tesla driver plea with police after FSD drove 64 mph in a 45
content:
A police department in Parker, Colorado, pulled over a Tesla going 64 mph in a 45 mph zone whose driver insisted they weren’t responsible, because the car was running “Full Self-Driving.”
Of course, Tesla will never take responsibility for that incident, but the frustrating part is that Tesla already has the solution and yet it refuses to implement it.
“These systems are designed to assist you, not drive for you”
The Parker Police Department shared the stop in a video this week. The driver’s excuse, as the department told it: “I wasn’t driving. I had auto assist on.” They were adamant enough to demand a supervisor.
The department’s reply was blunt. “Driver assistance technology does not replace the driver,” it said. “Whether your vehicle has adaptive cruise control, lane centering or full self-driving, you are still legally responsible for operating your vehicle safely.”
Legally, that isn’t close. Every driver-assist system you can buy in a new car today is a Level 2 system, which means the human is driving and the software is helping. Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” is Level 2. The name says one thing. The fine print, and the law, say another.
Tesla wants the name without the responsibility
Here’s the real problem, and it belongs to Tesla more than to the driver. Tesla sells a $99-a-month package called “Full Self-Driving.” Its CEO has spent a decade telling people the cars can basically drive themselves, and late last year Musk claimed FSD drivers can now text and drive.
But when something goes wrong, Tesla’s position flips. Suddenly the system is only “supervised,” the driver was always responsible, and the manual always said to keep your hands on the wheel.
So Tesla gets to market the car as self-driving and disclaim it as a mere driver aid, depending on which is more convenient in the moment. A driver at a traffic stop pointing at his dashboard is just that contradiction showing up on the side of the road.
The speeding isn’t a glitch. Tesla removed the fix
This is where Tesla loses credibility when it comes to FSd speeding: Tesla was speeding because Tesla designed FSD to drive over the limit, and then took away the tool owners used to rein it in.
I know this one first-hand. Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving” got me a ticket last month. In FSD v14, Tesla scrapped the adjustable speed offset that used to let drivers cap how far over the limit the car would go, and replaced it with fixed presets: Sloth, Chill, Standard, Hurry, and Mad Max. On a 50 km/h road in Standard mode, my car accelerated itself to 78 km/h, 28 over, with my foot nowhere near the pedal. A radar unit did the rest. With the old offset, I’d have set it to +15 and stayed out of trouble.
That’s the “easy fix” owners keep asking for: let the driver set a hard cap. Tesla’s head of AI, Ashok Elluswamy, has now said the company won’t do it, calling a user-set speed limit an “anti-pattern” and arguing Tesla would rather make FSD “smarter” than let owners override it. Tesla is supposed to make FSD smarter for a decade. The car meanwhile still ships with a mode literally named “Mad Max” that deliberately blows past speed limits, while you can’t trust ‘Standard mode’ to stay under the limit.
Regulators have noticed. Sweden told the EU to reject Tesla’s “FSD” unless the speeding behavior is removed. The gap between a product called “Full Self-Driving” and a car that knowingly breaks the speed limit is not a small one.
Electrek’s Take
To be clear, the driver’s excuse is absurd, and I have no problem with Parker police writing the ticket. If your car is speeding, you’re speeding. A cop is not going to cite your software subscription. When I got my ticket last month, I didn’t even mention FSD to the cop and just took the ticket.
Top comment by Damon Ekstrom
While I agree that the driver's excuse is absurd, I think this also shows why FSD will never see full autonomy, at least not in consumer vehicles.
I remember having to deactivate FSD multiple times, because my Model 3 would repeatedly blow past the speed limit. Once Tesla took away the ability to control the speed of the car, I knew I was going to have to be more alert than ever before. It was bad enough being on edge, worrying that the car would drive appropriately, but then I had to start worrying about whether I would get a speeding ticket. because the car now viewed speed limit signs as a suggestion.
Again, this is why FSD will always be a level 2 aid.
But I’m tired of the pile-on that stops at the driver, because Tesla built this confusion on purpose and profits from it. You cannot name a Level 2 system “Full Self-Driving,” tell people they can text behind the wheel, design the thing to drive over the speed limit, and then hide behind “the driver is always responsible” when the radar goes off. Pick one.
There’s an easy fix sitting right there, give owners back a hard speed cap, and Tesla is refusing it on principle and calling driver control an “anti-pattern.” That’s a company telling you it knows better than the driver and the posted limit both.
If Tesla wants drivers to take full responsibility for FSD, the least it could do is give them back the controls to drive it responsibly. Right now it’s doing the opposite.

title: Tesla starts Megapack 3 production with 28% more energy per unit
content:
Tesla Megapack
Fred Lambert
| Aug 6 2026 - 5:52 am PT
Tesla has started building its next-generation Megapack 3 grid battery, with the first units rolling off the line at the company’s new Megafactory in Brookshire, Texas.
The plant went from groundbreaking to production in 16 months and is designed to build 50 GWh of Megapack 3 a year. That’s the version Tesla says packs roughly 28% more energy into the same footprint as the Megapack it replaces.
Tesla confirmed the production start on Wednesday through its Megapack account, noting the Brookshire facility has “a designed capacity of 50 GWh/year dedicated to Megapack 3.” It’s the physical follow-through on the
Megapack 3 and Megablock reveal
Megapack 3 is officially rolling off the line at our newest Megafactory in Brookshire, Texas!
The factory went from groundbreaking to operation in just 16 months & has a designed capacity of 50 GWh/year dedicated to Megapack 3
So here’s what actually changed between Megapack 3 and the versions before it.
What’s different about Megapack 3
A single Megapack 3 holds about 5 MWh, up from 3.9 MWh on the Megapack 2 XL. That’s roughly 28% more storage in a box that takes up the same ground.
Tesla gets there mainly by using bigger cells. Megapack 3 moves to a larger 2.8-liter cell format, which lets Tesla cram more capacity into each cabinet without growing the enclosure.
The other big change is plumbing. Tesla says Megapack 3 cuts thermal-system connection points by 78% versus the previous generation. Fewer connections means fewer places for a liquid-cooled battery to leak or fail, and less labor to assemble and service. Not glamorous. But at grid scale, reliability and install time are the whole game.
For context, the Megapack has been climbing this curve for years. It launched in 2019 at around 3 MWh, then Tesla
squeezed it up to 3.9 MWh
with the 2 XL in 2022. Megapack 3 is the biggest single jump yet.
The real shift is the Megablock
A Megablock bundles up to four Megapack 3 units (about 20 MWh) with the transformer and switchgear already integrated at the factory. On older Megapacks, a lot of that medium-voltage wiring happened in the field, one of the slowest and most expensive parts of building a battery farm.
Tesla just signed a
$5 billion, 25 GWh Megapack deal with NatPower
in Europe, and data-center operators are buying storage as fast as Tesla can build it. A denser unit that goes up faster is exactly what those customers are asking for.
Why the new factory matters
Brookshire is Tesla’s answer to a supply problem. The company’s Lathrop, California Megafactory and its Shanghai plant have been running flat out, and Tesla
announced this third Megafactory
specifically to add capacity as competition from CATL, Fluence, and BYD heats up.
At 50 GWh a year dedicated to Megapack 3, Brookshire could quickly become Tesla’s largest energy storage manufacturing facility, beating Lathrop’s full output on its own. And building it in 16 months is fast for a facility this size.
Electrek’s Take
It’s impressive how quickly Tesla can get a new factory to production.
However, the spec that matters most with Megapack 3 isn’t the 5 MWh. It’s the Megablock. Grid batteries don’t fail to get built because the cells aren’t good enough — they stall on interconnection, permitting, and the slow, expensive work of wiring gear in a field. Moving that into the factory is the kind of unglamorous manufacturing win that actually moves deployment numbers, and it’s the same playbook Tesla ran on the Supercharger and that turned out more than alright.
The open question is cells. Tesla needs a lot of large-format cells to fill a 50 GWh factory, and a chunk of that still depends on suppliers and on how the current US tariff picture shakes out for imported LFP.
Tesla has already started reporting lower gross margins on its energy business due to high tariffs on LFP cells, and its own production isn’t coming close to 50 GWh.

title: World's first sodium-ion electric haul truck gets to work in China
content:
Electric Heavy Machinery
Sodium-ion Battery
Jo Borrás
| Aug 6 2026 - 5:01 am PT
While Americans fret over whether or not electric vehicles are up to the challenge of hauling them back and forth to the Piggly Wiggly
, Tonly is putting a fleet of advanced sodium battery electric haul trucks to work mining heavy ore.
Co-developed by Chinese equipment brand Tonly Heavy Industry and the chemistry experts at Hina Battery, the prototype 676 kWh “Haixing” series batteries fitted in this Tonly K120E electric haul truck deployed at the Tangshan Sanyou limestone mines are a world’s-first, offering super fast 0% to 100% charging times in under minutes over a usable lifespan of a positively massive 8,000 cycles (!) without the geopolitical headaches of lithium.
The Haixing batteries also offer respectable energy density specs at 165 Wh/kg, improved thermal stability (read: fire safety) compared to lithium, and –
the killer app for ultra class haul trucks
– superior cold-weather performance.
Cold blooded
Tonly haul truck at Peruvian mine; via Tonly.
These trucks are earmarked to work in the coldest regions of northern China,
where nighttime temperatures can frequently plummet to -20°C in areas like Harbin and Shenyang
. Those extreme temperatures don’t just wreak havoc on conventional lithium-ion battery range, they make it almost impossible for the big diesel engines that these big BEVs are replacing to even
let alone run efficiently
That’s why just about everyone who tests EVs in extreme cold comes out impressed with their performance compared to diesel. That includes semi trucks, light-duty BEVs, and (of course)
electric school buses
“Most of the winter it’s 30 to 35 below (zero),” offered West Grand County School District Director of Transportation, Bethany Aurinwhen, in a 2024 interview. “When it’s up to 20 below that’s good day, and (the electric school bus)
has performed extremely well
Putting people first
Autonomous Tonly haul trucks.
The sort of extreme temperatures that cripple diesels don’t just slow down a mine’s operations, they put the people behind the wheel of these massive machines at serious safety risk from cold-related injuries like frostbite and hypothermia.
That’s why stories like last month’s announcement that Tonly will deliver 800 autonomous TLE135 mining trucks to Xinjiang Hanxiang matter so much
Lower emissions, less pollution, reduced hearing loss from diesel drone, superior safety, and autonomous, all-weather performance. That’s a value proposition that’s going to be tough to beat – which explains just about every single political lobbying dollar being spent by the oil companies right now.
Gas and oil knows they’re beat.

title: Juiced doubles down with 120-mile range e-bike on dual-battery Scrambler Hardtail
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 6 2026 - 4:56 am PT
When Juiced Bikes
unveiled its new generation
of Scrambler models earlier this summer, the company hinted that an even longer-range version was on the way. Now it’s here.
Juiced has officially launched the dual-battery version of its Scrambler Hardtail, giving riders a claimed range of up to 120 miles (200 km) while keeping the same moped-style design that has made the Scrambler one of the company’s signature models – and the first model to relaunch the brand’s second act.
The new setup essentially doubles down on what many riders already liked about the 52V bike. A second battery mounted beneath the frame boosts total battery capacity to 38.4 Ah, helping push the claimed maximum range to 120 miles (200 km) under ideal riding conditions. That should make range anxiety all but disappear for commuters, weekend explorers, or anyone who just likes taking the scenic route home.
Of course, very few riders are actually going to pedal for 120 miles in a single outing. That number is based on ideal conditions with conservative riding. But the bigger takeaway isn’t necessarily the headline range figure – it’s the freedom that comes with having enough battery capacity that you can stop worrying about it altogether.
And even for riders who don’t intend to keep the bike in its lowest power mode to eke out that full 120 miles of range, the 1,996 Wh of capacity from those two batteries is going to provide plenty of high-power throttle riding, too.
Dual batteries offer twice the range
The bike still uses the same 1,764W peak rear hub motor found on the standard Hardtail Scrambler and meets the same legal requirements for Class 2 or Class 3 operation, meaning riders aren’t getting extra speed, but they are getting a lot more time in the saddle before needing to recharge.
Juiced is currently offering the dual-battery Hardtail Scrambler
for $1,999
, a $245 discount from its listed MSRP. The company is also throwing in a handful of accessories, including fenders, a handlebar bag, bar pad, headplate, custom nameplate, and stickers.
I recently had the chance
to spend time riding and reviewing the new Scrambler lineup
, and one of the things that stood out most was how well these bikes blend classic minibike styling with genuinely useful everyday performance. The Hardtail version skips rear suspension in favor of a simpler, lighter frame, though the large 20×4-inch tires still do a respectable job of soaking up rough pavement. And since its geometry has been carried over from the full-suspension version, it still rides like a well thought out, powerful e-bike – not a random Amazon frame with a motor strapped on.
With a second battery, you’ll never let your girl see your range anxiety
For riders who regularly rack up serious mileage or simply hate charging, the dual-battery Scrambler looks like a compelling new option.
At under $2,000
, it also undercuts many other long-range e-bikes while bringing a unique moto-inspired style that has become something of a Juiced trademark.

title: Latvia’s solar capacity surpasses 1.5 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Latvia has installed around 600 MW of solar so far this year, meaning 2026 has already broken the country’s record for solar deployed in a calendar year. Solar was Latvia’s largest source of electricity in May and June, with figures for July yet to be released.
Patrick Jowett
06 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Image: Kaspars Upmanis/Unsplash
Latvia’s solar capacity has reached 1,521 MW, according to figures shared by the Latvian Renewable Energy Alliance (LREA).
The figure indicates around 601 MW of solar have been added in the country so far this year, adding to the
that were installed by the end of the last year. This growth trajectory means 2026 is already the most successful year for solar deployment in Latvia, outpacing the previous calendar record year of 319 MW in 2024.
LREA member and Head of Business Development at Evecon, Gatis Macāns, told
pv magazine
that the expansion of Latvia’s renewable energy sector is being driven by the completion of large-scale solar projects that were initiated several years ago, as well as continued investment in distributed generation and rapid deployment of wind and battery energy storage systems.
“These developments are expected to further strengthen the country’s renewable generation capacity and support the ongoing energy transition,” Macāns said.
There have been five new solar power parks with a combined connection capacity of 519 MW connected to Latvia’s transmission system operator (TSO) network during 2026 so far, Macāns shared, as well as 150 MW of wind across two projects and two battery storage systems totaling 68 MW of capacity.
Details published by Latvian TSO Augstsprieguma tīkls (AST) says these connected solar projects consist of a 110 MW solar park in Ventspils, a 199 MW facility in the South Kurzeme municipality, a 40 MW project in Valmiera, a 60 MW site in Madona and 110 MW project in Krāslava.
AST adds that it plans to connect four more wind farms and four hybrid solar-plus-storage parks with a combined capacity of 913 MW by the end of the year. The TSO also forecasts that, based on connection agreements for new grid connections, the capacity of solar and wind connected to the TSO network, which now exceeds 1.1 GW, could double over the next three years.
There is an additional 782 MW of utility-scale solar now connected to Latvia’s distribution system operator (DSO) network, Macāns added, while microgenerators, consisting of systems up to 11.1 kW in size, now represent around 220 MW of installed capacity, around a 10 MW increase on figures from the end of last year.
“In the small-scale segment, several support programmes remain available for households, municipalities and companies investing in self-consumption solar projects, supporting continued growth in distributed PV installations,” Macāns added.
A report from Latvian DSO, Sadales tīkls, says solar accounts for 78% of the total generation capacity installed in the distribution network, while the volume of solar energy produced increased by 50% compared to the first six months of last year, with 441.3 GWh of solar electricity fed into the grid this year alone.
Latvia’s strong solar growth over the first half of this year helped solar become the country’s largest source of electricity in both May and June, with final figures for July yet to be released.
Data released by AST says solar generated 274 GWh in Latvia in June, 55% of the 495 GWh of total electricity generation. Hydropower was the second largest form of electricity, generating 158 GWh. In June, Latvian electricity production provided 88.48% of total national electricity consumption.
Latvia’s share of solar within its domestic electricity generation in June was an
EU record
, according to separate analysis by Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE.
Additional reporting by AST says that across the first half of 2026, electricity generation in Latvia exceeded consumption by 7%. Renewable energy power plants currently account for 71% of the total capacity of power plants connected to the transmission network.

title: Finnish push for data center flexibility - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Green energy parks combining renewables grid supply with onsite generation, energy storage and energy management software can enable data centers to participate positively in the energy market. Seppo Ihalianen told
pv magazine
how Finland’s ecogrid.energy is implementing this approach, beginning with a 300 MW project.
Blathnaid O’Dea
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
Image: Vattenfall
Optimization software, onsite renewables (green energy parks) and tailored design models are some of the demand-side response ideas being tested out on data centers.
Finnish founder and executive director Seppo Ihalainen believes in a combination of all the above approaches – and that’s why he founded ecogrid.energy.
Headquartered in Pori, Finland, the early-stage company’s business model has three main strands, each addressing a different part of the data center grid interaction puzzle.
Ecogrid is building its first green energy park in Pori with Norwegian data center developer ASP Data Centers who will own and run the 300 MW facility. Another larger design facility, the Raisio model, is planned to start construction in 2030. Ecogrid designs the energy parks together with its engineering and construction partners.
The energy park model combines renewables grid supply with onsite generation and energy storage, with a pathway to biogas, synthetic fuels and green hydrogen as they become commercially feasible, said Ihalainen.
The company has also developed a proprietary hybrid energy management software platform called EMOP which Ihalainen said acts as “the link between the energy market and the data center infrastructure.” The Pori energy park will be the first facility to deploy the EMOP system, which is currently optimized for the NordPool energy market.
“We are a young company evolving together with this project, although we have a long history of data centers and there are data centers in Finland using EMOP-like functionalities. We have been involved in their development,” the founder told
pv magazine
Ihalainen and Ecogrid’s CEO, Antti Hänninen, are aiming to make the optimization software and green energy park combination a standard across all data center developments in the future where possible. Ecogrid is actively looking to expand into other markets, and it has a subsidiary in Singapore focused on Southeast Asia. It is also providing advisory services to Chinese AI companies to help them with excess heat reuse.
According to Ihalainen, bringing EMOP to countries with more monopolized markets is challenging as it requires an open market, but he is confident that as more renewable energy is introduced on the system a traditionally monopolized market can “correct itself and become more open.”
Besides Southeast Asia, Ecogrid is targeting Ireland. In fact, the idea for the Ecogrid model first came to Ihalainen two years ago when he was attending a data center industry forum in Ireland. “There was a lot of conversations about data centers needing to be a power asset but at that point it was difficult to build data centers on the island because there was no power,” he recalled.
He was referring to the moratorium on new grid connections for data centers in the Irish capital, Dublin, that was introduced in 2021 due to severe grid bottlenecks. “And we started thinking, what would need to be done to change data center design and how they could be able to participate in the energy market,” said Ihalainen.
The Irish data center moratorium was later lifted in Dec. 2025 and replaced with a policy allowing data centers to connect to the grid only if they prove they can provide 80% of their power needs with new onsite energy generation.
Tiered approach
Meanwhile, Finland has a tiered approach whereby data centers that create value through energy market participation and district heating programs are favored first, followed by traditional hyperscalers that don’t generate much value for society but rely on external resources and are able to bring their own financing with them. The lowest priority is the third category: data centers that use cheap electricity, draining the national grid and contributing nothing.
Finland also removed electricity tax advantages for data centers, moving them from the lower industrial tariff to the higher electricity tax bracket. Finland’s grid is relatively easy to connect to compared to many other European markets.
Ihalainen said Finland’s energy system is also better prepared than Ireland’s was for more data center builds, with more than 95% fossil fuel-free.
Ecogrid CEO Anti Hänninen said that while it’s important to incentivize what he called good data centers, introducing one uniform renewables mandate might not be the best way to do this. Offering a special grid connection package for data centers on a tailored basis is better and would generate more competition among data center developers to meet renewables requirements in a way that works for everyone.
Finland’s data center industry is not as big as Ireland’s, but it is growing fast and managing flexibility needs to happen now. “It is justified to encourage and, if necessary, even require data centers to make use of flexibility,” Riku Huttunen, Director-General of the Energy Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment in Finland
“Market prices guide data centers to actively utilize their battery storages and reserve capacity – which they have built for securing server operations – to balance costs. This incentive becomes more obvious when obtaining an affordable fixed-price electricity contract turns out to be increasingly difficult,” he added in a column outlining the Finnish government’s position. “The option of prioritizing operators planning to connect to the network based on objective criteria and within the framework of EU legislation should be assessed. The idea is to enable the operators with less network and electricity load to access the grid faster. One particular criterion could be flexible electricity use.”
Finland’s grid operator, Fingrid, requires data centers larger than 30 MW to be able to flex 30% of its consumption in real time. When Fingrid sends a time-sensitive signal to turn down by 30%, EMOP relays this to the operator to start their power production or switch off, depending on the model.

title: Ørsted turns on 500 MWh battery project with co-located solar in Texas - pv magazine Global
content:

The Old 300 Storage project has reached commercial operations and is now fully integrated with the ERCOT grid, using made-in-America Tesla battery energy storage systems (BESS). It is co-located with a 430 MW solar project that was switched on in 2024.
Matthew Lynas
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
United States
Utility-scale
Image: Ørsted
The 250 MW/500 MWh Old 300 Storage project in Needville, Texas, co-located with a 430 MW solar project, has reached commercial operations, according to Danish multinational energy company Ørsted.
Old 300 Storage is fully integrated into the ERCOT grid and will be operated independently from the Old 300 Solar installation, which has been generating since 2024.
The Energy storage facility comprises Tesla Megapacks manufactured at the company’s Lathrop, California facility. Ørsted said the developer and Tesla have been working in collaboration with the Needville Fire Department to provide “comprehensive education” on the energy storage technology and safety response protocols.
Melissa Peterson, president of Ørsted Americas Onshore, noted that BESS has been playing a larger role on the ERCOT grid, providing power at times of tight supply and demand margins.
“Achieving commercial operations at our Old 300 Storage project will have tangible benefits, such as strengthening grid reliability by providing additional resources to Texas grid operators and allowing for more diverse and localized energy options as electricity demand continues to grow,” Peterson said.
Old 300 Storage is part of a growing onshore portfolio developed by Ørsted in the United States. Major projects include a
300MW/1200MWh BESS
located developed with Salt River Project and located alongside the Eleven Mile Solar Center in Pinal County, Arizona. The project was commissioned in 2024 and represented an approximate $1 billion investment by Ørsted in clean energy for Arizona.
Following the Old 300 BESS entering commercial operations, Ørsted now has 6 GW of operational onshore US energy projects. The developer estimates the Old 300 solar and storage projects will inject approximately $110 million combined in property tax revenue for the local area.

title: South Korea proceeds with largest single-site PV project to date - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The 400 MW solar complex, scheduled for completion in 2028, is expected to supply 529 GWh of electricity annually. The project will include a 10 MW agrivoltaics array.
Patrick Jowett
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
South Korea
Utility-scale
Image: William Warby/Unsplash
A groundbreaking ceremony for South Korea’s largest solar complex to date will take place tomorrow (August 7).
The 400 MW Haenam solar power complex, to be located in the south of the country, will be built on approximately 4.79 million square metres of idle land, including reclaimed saline land. Earlier this year, Korea South-East Power Co. (KOEN) was selected as the preferred engineering, procurement and construction bidder for the project.
The site is expected to be completed in 2028. Once operational, it will supply 529 GWh of electricity annually – equivalent to the consumption of around 130,000 Korean households – to companies and industrial complexes that have adopted 100% renewable energy targets.
South Korea’s Minister of Climate, Energy and Environment, Kim Sung-hwan, commented that the project forms part of the ministry’s plan to lower power generation costs by expanding the supply of large-scale renewable energy projects on idle sites of land.
The project will be built using domestically-produced solar modules, cells and inverters, according to an update posted by the ministry. In May, Korean manufacturer Hanwha QCells announced it had been selected to supply cells and modules required for the project, produced at the company’s plant in the province of North Chungcheong.
The project also plans to establish a resident participation and profit-sharing system. The mechanism will enable local residents to participate in the project by sharing power generation profits with the local community. The ministry says this will ensure a total KRW 150 billion ($105.2 million) in power generation profits is returned to the local community during the project period.
Similar profit-sharing modules have been undertaken in former utility-scale PV projects in South Korea, such as the
47.2 MW Ihma Dam solar project
, finished last November, which is the country’s largest floating PV array located alongside a multi-purpose dam.
The ministry’s latest update also confirms 10 MW of the Haenam complex will be developed as agricultural solar power. The country passed its
first dedicated agrivoltaics legislation
earlier this year.
South Korea’s cumulative solar capacity reached 30,346 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), a 3.6 GW increase on figures reported at the end of 2024.
In July, it announced its latest solar tender covering
1 GW of new solar capacity
with a bid ceiling price of KRW 147,686/kWh.

The government of the Philippines is preparing a new procurement exercise under its flagship green energy auction (GEA) program that will specifically target agrisolar and projects integrated with aquaculture, referred to by the government as aquasolar.
The country’s Department of Energy (DOE) and Department of Agriculture have reviewed a draft memorandum of understanding for the auction, which is scheduled to be the 9th (GEA-9) under the program.
A statement published by DOE says agrisolar and aquasolar installations can optimize abandoned, underdeveloped and underutilized land and water resources while supporting food security and rural livelihoods.
“By integrating renewable energy with agriculture and aquaculture, GEA-9 aims to enable innovative projects that deliver clean power alongside sustainable farming and fishing,” the department’s statement adds.
“The official publication of the GEA-9 Terms of Reference is targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026, marking another step toward a resilient, multi-sectoral clean energy transition.”
The Philippines’ GEA is a competitive bidding program aimed at private investors. In February, DOE announced plans to hold its next four green energy auctions, GEA-6 to GEA-9, over the next two years as part of wider plans to auction
25 GW of renewables
announced in April
, will cover rooftop solar, ground-mounted solar and floating solar technologies, with the floating solar allocation expected to incorporate unsubscribed capacities from the fourth green energy auction, which wrapped up
last November
Earlier this week, DOE announced a future round of the GEA will be dedicated to off-grid areas served by the state-run National Power Corporation. It will look to procure renewable energy facilities with battery energy storage systems to replace existing diesel-fired power plants.
The department said the off-grid auction will specifically target 20 islands, with the longlist still to be finalized. The auction is currently scheduled to run next year.

title: Researchers compare PV, wind, hybrid systems for community-scale energy - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in China found a hybrid system combining 200 kW of PV, 200 kW of wind and a 100 kWh battery achieved a 70.8% self-sufficiency rate for a community consuming 1,000 kWh per day. While standalone PV delivered a lower levelized cost of energy, the hybrid configuration offered the best overall balance between cost and supply reliability.
Lior Kahana
06 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Image: pv magazine / AI generated
A research group in China has conducted an integrated techno-economic-environmental assessment of a grid-connected PV-wind hybrid system for community-scale energy applications. The findings are presented in the paper
Designing and evaluating the grid-connected hybrid PV-WT-battery system from techno-economic perspectives
, published in
Case Studies in Thermal Engineering.
The study compared three grid-connected community energy systems, each with 400 kW of renewable generation capacity and a 100 kWh lithium-ion battery. The three configurations comprised a 400 kW PV system, a 400 kW wind system and a hybrid system combining 200 kW of PV with 200 kW of wind.
Each wind turbine was rated at 20 kW, while the PV system had a module efficiency of 17.3%, a 90% derating factor, a 25-year service life and a converter efficiency of 98%. The battery operated between 20% and 100% state of charge.
The study modeled the systems in the Chinese city of Karamay, northern Xinjiang, and Kashgar in southwestern Xinjiang, with an average electricity demand of 1,000 kWh per day, or approximately 365 MWh per year. The systems were simulated over a representative full year using 8,760 hourly values for solar radiation, wind speed, ambient temperature and electricity demand.
Renewable electricity first met community demand, with surplus generation used to charge the battery before any remaining electricity was exported to the grid. When renewable output was insufficient, the battery discharged before electricity was imported from the grid.
Grid electricity prices were CNY 0.24 ($0.036)/kWh during off-peak periods, CNY 0.40/kWh during standard periods, and CNY 0.59/kWh during peak periods, while exported electricity received CNY 0.262/kWh. The economic analysis assumed a 20-year project lifetime, a 5% nominal discount rate, 3% inflation, PV capital costs of CNY 3,500/kW, wind costs of CNY 4,000/kW, and battery costs of CNY 1,000/kWh.
The results show that the standalone PV system achieved the lowest levelized cost of energy (LCOE), at CNY 0.189/kWh, compared with CNY 0.237/kWh for the PV-wind hybrid system and CNY 0.291/kWh for the standalone wind system.
However, the hybrid system provided the best overall balance between economic performance and supply reliability, achieving the highest self-sufficiency rate (SSR) of 70.8% and requiring only 106.7 MWh/year of grid electricity. By comparison, the standalone PV and wind systems achieved SSRs of 58.2% and 58.0%, respectively, while requiring 152.6 MWh/year and 153.2 MWh/year of grid electricity.
The researchers found that resource availability strongly influenced performance. “Karamay exhibits higher SSR and lower LCOE but suffers from stronger curtailment, while Kashgar maintains higher self-consumption rate but lower SSR and weaker economic competitiveness,” they explained.
They added that their assessment provides “a theoretical basis and engineering guidance for the optimal allocation and operation of regional hybrid energy systems.”
Scientists from China’s
Xinjiang University
Chongqing University
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
contributed to the research.

title: Brazil proposes mandatory take-back scheme for solar panels, batteries - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A bill under review in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies stipulates that manufacturers, importers and retailers should be responsible for collecting and recycling equipment after its end-of-life.
Alessandra Neris
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Americas
Batteries
Image: Mateus Campos Felipe/Unsplash
A bill currently being processed in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies aims to make reverse logistics mandatory for photovoltaic panels, batteries and energy storage systems.
The proposal seeks to anticipate one of the main environmental challenges associated with the expansion of solar power generation and energy storage: the proper disposal of equipment at the end of its useful life.
Bill 753/2026 establishes that manufacturers, importers and retailers must collect and send discarded consumer equipment for recycling or environmentally appropriate disposal. The text also incorporates these products into the reverse logistics system foreseen in the country’s National Solid Waste Policy (PNRS).
According to the proposal, collection systems should be structured by the sector itself, without using the public urban cleaning service. Installation companies will also assume additional responsibilities, including guiding consumers on how to return equipment and receiving modules, batteries and components replaced during maintenance services to forward to licensed recycling units.
The proposal also features ecodesign criteria, stipulating that equipment should be developed to facilitate disassembly and reuse of materials, as well as reduce the use of potentially hazardous substances.
In the proposal’s justification, its author, Representative Clodoaldo Magalhães, states that the accelerated growth of solar energy requires the creation of such mechanisms to avoid environmental problems in the coming decades.
According to Magalhães, studies indicate that Brazil could generate around 550,000 tons of photovoltaic panel waste over the next few years, making it necessary to create a structured chain for the collection and reuse of these materials.
The bill will be reviewed by the committees on Environment and Sustainable Development, Urban Development, and Constitution, Justice and Citizenship. If approved by the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, it will proceed to presidential sanction before coming into effect.

title: India targets 5 GW of floating PV with co-located storage - pv magazine Global
content:

A newly-approved government scheme in India plans to support the development of 5 GW of floating solar on existing reservoirs and industrial ponds, to be paired with energy storage systems with a minimum storage capacity of two hours.
Uma Gupta
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Highlights
