Image: Tata Power
The Indian government has approved a INR 50.7 billion ($533 million) program to support the deployment of 5 GW of floating solar PV projects paired with energy storage systems.
The scheme, known as Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY), aims to expand floating solar capacity by utilizing existing reservoirs and industrial ponds, in turn reducing competition for scarce land resources while improving grid reliability through integrated energy storage.
It will target 5 GW of floating solar with co-located energy storage systems with a minimum storage capacity of two hours. The projects are expected to be sanctioned from financial years (FY) 2026-27 to 2030-31, with disbursement of financial support continuing up to FY 2032-33.
The program will offer central finance assistance of INR 10 million/MW for eligible floating solar photovoltaic projects after successful commissioning, as well as up to INR 5 million per project to cover feasibility studies, including bathymetry and hydrography assessments, environmental studies, and other preparatory activities required for de-risking project development.
The approval follows a recent assessment undertaken by India’s National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE), which estimated the country’s floating solar potential at approximately 102.18 GWp across reservoirs and other suitable inland water bodies .
India currently has around 700 MW of installed floating solar PV capacity.

title: Agrivoltaics improve grape quality in Mediterranean rainfed vineyards - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Italy found that agrivoltaic shading in Primitivo vineyards can reduce heat and water stress while improving vine physiology, growth, biodiversity, and yield under Mediterranean conditions. The study shows that photovoltaic integration can enhance vineyard resilience and maintain grape quality, although further long-term and multi-site research is needed to confirm its wider applicability.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Utility-scale
Image: Hector Uribe / Unsplash
Researchers from the
University of Bari Aldo Moro
in Italy Researchers have investigated the effects of photovoltaic-induced shading on vineyards of Primitivo, a traditional grape variety cultivated in the Apulia region. The study examines how partial shading from photovoltaic panels influences vine growth, microclimatic conditions, and grape production, providing insights into the potential integration of solar energy systems with viticulture.
“The objective is to assess whether agrivoltaic integration can mitigate the effects of high temperatures and water deficit, thereby improving grapevine adaptability in Mediterranean environments,” the scientists stated.
The experiment was conducted during the 2024 growing season in a commercial agrivoltaic vineyard located at the “Le Rene” solar farm in Laterza, southern Italy. The agrivoltaic system covered 8,812 m² with a photovoltaic capacity of 350 kW, while a nearby full-sun area served as the control. Three light treatments were established: full sun (FS, 100% irradiance), low shade (LS, approximately 95% irradiance between panel rows), and high shade (HS, approximately 5% irradiance beneath the panels).
Continuous monitoring of microclimatic parameters, including air and soil temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, wind speed, and vapor pressure deficit, was performed using automated weather stations. Vine physiological responses were assessed throughout the growing season through measurements of stomatal conductance, leaf temperature, chlorophyll content, fluorescence, photosynthesis, transpiration, and water status.
Light quality and quantity were also characterized using spectral measurements of photosynthetically active radiation and the red-to-far-red ratio. Growth and morphological traits, including shoot development, leaf area, biomass accumulation, and stomatal characteristics, were evaluated through destructive sampling.
The study also investigated the impact of photovoltaic shading on spontaneous vegetation by comparing plant diversity and community composition beneath the panels and in the full-sun vineyard area using floristic surveys and diversity indices. At harvest, yield components and grape quality parameters were analyzed, including cluster number, cluster weight, berry composition, total soluble solids, pH, titratable acidity, polyphenol content, and anthocyanin profiles.
The analysis showed that the agrivoltaic system significantly modified the vineyard microclimate, vine physiology, growth, biodiversity, and grape quality. Shading reduced air temperature by approximately 0.5–1 C, increased relative humidity by up to 14%, and improved soil moisture compared with FS conditions, indicating a buffering effect against summer heat and drought stress. Physiological measurements revealed higher chlorophyll content, improved photochemical efficiency, and better water status under shaded conditions, particularly under HS, while LS maintained higher photosynthetic activity.
The altered light environment strongly affected vine morphology, with shaded vines producing longer shoots, larger leaves, thicker stems and petioles, and greater biomass accumulation than FS vines. Shading also increased stomatal density and modified stomatal characteristics, suggesting long-term physiological acclimation to reduced radiation. Floristic surveys showed that species richness beneath the photovoltaic panels was approximately twice that of the full-sun area, indicating that the agrivoltaic system created a more favourable microhabitat for spontaneous vegetation.
Yield components were positively affected by shading, with LS and HS treatments increasing cluster number, cluster weight, and yield per cane compared with FS vines. Although full-sun grapes reached slightly higher sugar concentrations, shaded grapes maintained adequate ripening parameters, higher acidity, and improved polyphenolic accumulation, especially under LS conditions.
Overall, the results demonstrate that agrivoltaic shading can enhance vine resilience, improve productivity, support biodiversity, and maintain grape quality in Mediterranean rainfed vineyards.
“These results indicate that agrivoltaic systems can influence vineyard functioning at multiple levels,” the researchers concluded. “However, long-term and multi-site evaluations are required to verify the responses in different climatic conditions, for more seasons and also with other fruit species.”
The research work can be found in “
Agrivoltaics in Mediterranean viticulture: Impacts on physiology, yield andm biodiversity
,” published in
Scientia Horticulturae

title: US data centers turn to on-site solar, storage, VPPs as grid delays mount - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
A Reuters Events report highlights how multi-year transmission delays are forcing data center developers in the United States to deploy 56 GW of on-site generation while turning to Virtual Power Plants to unlock fast capacity.
Ryan Kennedy
06 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
United States
Utility-scale
Google Data Center, Council Bluffs Iowa | Image: Chad Davis / Flickr – CC BY 2.0
Rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centers, manufacturing, and electrification is colliding directly with long-standing grid interconnection bottlenecks across the United States. With long-distance transmission infrastructure taking up to 15 years to build, clean energy developers and tech hyperscalers are turning to on-site power and distributed energy resources to bridge the gap.
According to a
whitepaper
At the same time, grid interconnection queues reached over 2,200 GW of planned capacity in mid-2026, far surpassing the nation’s total installed capacity of 1,400 GW.
While investor-owned utilities plan $1.1 trillion in grid investments through 2029 and regional transmission operators (RTOs) like the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) and Midcontinent Independent System Operator build out 765 kV extra high-voltage backbones, those transmission lines face six- to seven-year buildouts.
This multi-year timeline mismatch is forcing a strategic shift for solar, energy storage, and distributed energy resource (DER) providers.
On-site solar and battery storage
To circumvent grid connection delays, data center developers are increasingly pursuing on-site power generation. Market intelligence data cited in the report indicates that developers were planning roughly 56 GW of on-site capacity as of early 2026, accounting for 30% of all planned data center builds nationwide.
Texas leads the trend with over 20.6 GW of planned behind-the-meter capacity, followed by New Mexico (9.2 GW), Pennsylvania (7.5 GW), and Utah (6.0 GW).
While natural gas accounts for a significant portion of interconnection queue requests in regions like SPP, the urgency for rapid deployment is creating major opportunities for co-located utility-scale solar and battery energy storage systems (BESS).
Grid operators are actively structuring policies to favor fast-tracked load. For example, SPP introduced its High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA) framework, offering connection agreements in under 90 days for data centers that bring their own generation to support their load.
VPPs and storage
Beyond co-located hardware, the report underscores the growing reliance on Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) and Grid-Enhancing Technologies (GETs) to release immediate capacity.
A Brattle Group study cited in the report notes that demand flexibility tools, including flexible distributed energy resources, smart thermostats, and battery storage, could unlock up to 200 GW of demand response capacity across utilities and wholesale markets
This dynamic is accelerating commercial partnerships between tech giants and residential solar/storage aggregators:
Sunrun, Tesla, and Renew Home announced plans for a 16 GW VPP, using aggregated home batteries and smart devices to supply dispatchable capacity and create grid headroom.
Google and Voltus partnered on a 3-year agreement to aggregate 100 MW of flexible assets to support regional utility capacity.
As greenfield transmission projects continue to contend with permitting and supply chain constraints, the ability to deploy behind-the-meter solar, quick-to-interconnect storage, and aggregated VPP capacity is moving from an alternative strategy to an essential path forward for powering U.S. digital infrastructure.

title: New US fusion fuel technology could power commercial fusion reactors
content: A US nuclear fusion company has secured a license to use four advanced fueling technologies developed by researchers at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) to advance commercial fusion reactors.The licensing agreement was signed on Wednesday, August 5, during the Nuclear Opportunities Workshop in Tennessee. Under the deal, Type One Energy will gain access to a suite of cryogenic pellet fueling technologies for fusion reactors.Fusion reactors generate energy by fusing hydrogen isotopes at extremely high temperatures. To maintain the reaction, they must be continuously supplied with fuel. One of the most effective methods is cryogenic pellet fueling. It forms solid hydrogen pellets just a few degrees above absolute zero, before injecting them into the plasma at high speed.The approach could deliver fuel deeper into the plasma than conventional gas injection technologies. “Our continuing collaboration with Oak Ridge National Laboratory is accelerating the commercialization of fusion energy,” John Canik, Type One Energy’s chief science and engineering officer, said.Improving reactor fuelingThe agreement covers four of the lab’s inventions that address challenges in fuel production, tritium handling, and stable reactor operation. The first is a tritium-compatible cryogenic pellet gas gun that fires tiny frozen hydrogen fuel pellets into the reactor’s plasma. It relies on materials that can safely handle radioactive tritium, adjusts pellet size in real time, and reduces wear and failures during long-term operation. The second invention is a tritium-compatible cryogenic screw extruder for plasma energy pellet injection. It continuously produces frozen fuel pellets while working safely with tritium. It keeps the radioactive fuel sealed in the system and supports different fuel mixtures, temperatures, and production rates.Type One Energy’s Matt Miles (L) and ORNL Director Stephen Streiffer signing the fusion technology licensing agreement.Credit: Alonda Hines / ORNL, U.S. Dept. of EnergyIn addition, the third invention is a pressure relief device that protects the fueling system from dangerous pressure buildup at temperatures below 20 kelvin (-423.7 degrees Fahrenheit). The reusable valve prevents damage to seals and improves the overall safety of the fueling system.Finally, the fourth technology is a closed-loop fuel recirculation system that can recover unused frozen fuel, convert it back into gas, and feed it into the pellet-making process. The system cuts fuel waste, limits radioactive inventory, and removes the need for separate gas-handling equipment. Sustaining fusion powerFusion reactors fueled by deuterium and tritium must be continuously refueled to replace the ions, which are consumed in the reaction and lost from the confining magnetic fields. Deuterium is abundant. In contrast, tritium is scarce, radioactive, and significantly more difficult to process safely. ORNL said current pellet injection systems cannot produce fuel pellets at the rates needed for commercial fusion reactors. The licensed technologies are intended to close that gap. Representatives from Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Type One Energy after the signing of the licensing agreement.Credit: Alonda Hines / ORNL, U.S. Dept. of EnergyThe technologies will support Type One Energy’s stellarator fusion power system, which uses complex magnetic fields to confine plasma. The firm has previously collaborated with ORNL on several fusion projects, including a high-heat-flux testing facility and work under the Department of Energy’s Innovation Network for Fusion Energy (INFUSE) program.Stephen Streiffer, ORNL director, said that Type One Energy is a valued partner in fusion research. “This license is an exciting next step in our partnership, moving our fueling research out of the lab and into application, and we look forward to seeing these technologies contribute to the future of fusion energy,” Streiffer concluded in a press release.

title: Firestorm Labs prints 1,000 parts, 12 drones aboard US Navy warship
content: Firestorm Labs has manufactured more than 1,000 components and assembled 12 Squall first-person-view drones aboard the USS Essex, demonstrating how military hardware could be produced during maritime operations. The two-week trial took place while the US Navy warship sailed from San Diego to Hawaii for RIMPAC 2026.Using its containerized xCell manufacturing platform, the US defense technology company produced drone components and repair parts despite waves reaching 12 feet. The deployment, organized through the Naval Postgraduate School CAMRE network and facilitated by FLEETWERX, aimed to reduce dependence on shore-based resupply while supporting repairs and combat readiness at sea.Manufacturing through rough seas on a warshipThe deployment was xCell’s first maritime demonstration under operational conditions. Instead of waiting for parts to be transported by aircraft, ship, or convoy, crews could manufacture equipment close to where it was required while remaining on station.Firestorm tested printer performance aboard the moving warship and produced three main categories of hardware: mechanical test pieces, components for Squall drones, and repair items requested by the crew.Operations continued in conditions reaching sea state 5, demonstrating production amid significant vessel movement.More than 20 crew-requested items were also manufactured. These included deck tie-down inspection gauges, reverse-engineered valve handwheels, electrical covers, cable hardware, door components, a Starlink deployment mount, and a nonconductive digging knife for explosive ordnance disposal teams.Protecting aircraft and supporting sailorsOne notable component was an Apache rotor guard droop stop designed during the first Army-Navy Apache operations conducted at sea. The device reduced the risk of the helicopter’s rotor striking the deck as the vessel moved through unusually heavy seas off Southern California.Firestorm said an Apache main rotor costs approximately $500,000, while damage from a blade striking the deck could cost $230,000 for each of its four blades. Manufacturing the protective component aboard the ship helped enable operations with the helicopter’s rotors mounted.The team also converted a sailor’s idea into a vacuum adapter for inflatable Life Preserving Units. Because no suitable connector was known to exist, Firestorm designed three versions for different vacuums and operating requirements.Drones move from ship to exerciseFirestorm assembled 12 Squall FPV drones during the voyage and later flew them at RIMPAC in Hawaii. Soldiers, sailors, and Marines received training in additive manufacturing, drone assembly, and flight operations.Marines from the 3rd Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion subsequently operated the drones as adversary aircraft during a three-day counter-UAS exercise at Makua Military Reservation on Oahu. The flights supported experimentation conducted for CAMRE during the multinational exercise.“The Indo-Pacific logistics problem is real, and most of the answers on offer live in a pitch deck,” said Dan Magy, CEO of Firestorm. “We printed flight-ready aircraft and the parts a crew actually needed, in the conditions they’d actually face. That’s what manufacturing at the edge looks like when it works,” he added. The demonstration indicates that deployable additive manufacturing could shorten repair timelines, keep vessels operational for longer, and allow US forces and allied partners to regenerate expendable drone capacity across contested maritime regions.

title: US Army backs shell that flies 65,000 feet, hits targets 93 miles away
content: Tiberius Aerospace has signed a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army to advance Sceptre, its precision-guided, ramjet-powered 155mm (about 6.1 inches) artillery munition.Announced on Thursday, the partnership brings the defense company together with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center to mature the weapon.The program seeks to extend the reach and precision of existing tube artillery without requiring militaries to purchase new launchers. Sceptre is designed to travel beyond Mach 3, climb above 65,000 feet, and strike targets up to 93 miles (150 kilometers) away, including in environments where GPS signals are unavailable or disrupted.Collaboration targets technical maturationThe agreement creates a framework through which Tiberius Aerospace and DEVCOM Armaments Center can conduct mutually approved research and technical work. Such agreements allow U.S. government laboratories and private companies to share expertise, facilities, and resources while developing technologies of common interest.For Tiberius, the arrangement represents another step in Sceptre’s development and expands its work with the U.S. Department of Defense. The effort will focus on validating and refining the technologies needed to turn the experimental round into a mature artillery capability.Sceptre differs from conventional rocket-assisted projectiles because its liquid-fueled ramjet delivers propulsion throughout its flight. This sustained thrust is intended to help the shell achieve greater speed, altitude, and range after being fired from a NATO-standard 155mm howitzer.The munition is designed to land within five meters of its target, according to the company. Its ability to operate without GPS could prove valuable in contested battlefields where satellite navigation faces jamming, spoofing, or other electronic interference.Existing howitzers gain longer reachA central feature of Sceptre is its compatibility with artillery systems already used by NATO forces. The round does not need a dedicated launcher or bespoke firing platform, potentially allowing militaries to expand their long-range firepower while retaining current howitzers.Its propulsion system can also use several readily available military fuels, including diesel, JP-4, and JP-8. By drawing on established battlefield fuel networks, the design is intended to reduce the storage, transportation, and sustainment burden associated with introducing a new type of munition.Tiberius reached a major development milestone in April 2026 when it launched a liquid-fueled ramjet from a NATO-standard 155mm howitzer. The company described it as a world-first demonstration.Software-defined shell evolves with threatsPrevious testing has examined whether the round can withstand launch forces of approximately 16,000 g. Tiberius has also demonstrated fin deployment and stable aerodynamic flight as part of a test campaign that evaluates Sceptre’s underlying systems separately before integrating them.The shell uses a modular, open software architecture intended to support upgrades during its operational life. Tiberius plans to connect it with GRAIL, an AI-powered platform developed to accelerate weapon-system improvements.Through GRAIL, engineers could introduce updated targeting functions, guidance algorithms, mission software, and autonomous capabilities as requirements change. The platform also links operational needs with engineering, testing, and distributed manufacturing, allowing the munition to respond more quickly to battlefield threats without replacing its fundamental hardware.

title: New sodium-ion battery skips mechanical cooling with 97.9% efficiency
content: Deploying grid-scale energy storage usually means battling extreme heat.To keep lithium-ion power plants from melting down or catching fire, energy companies pump massive amounts of power back into giant air conditioning units. It is an expensive, inefficient loop.Syntropic Power and UNIGRID Inc. think they have a better way, and it starts with table salt’s cousin.The two companies announced a major partnership to commercialize UNIGRID’s proprietary sodium chromium oxide (NaCrO₂) battery technology across North America, targeting one gigawatt-hour (1 GWh) of deployments in 2027.The technology could be used in residential, virtual power plant, and large-scale stationary grid applications.Chemistry distinction in sodium versus lithium batteryAlthough lithium-ion batteries entered commercial use in the 1990s. Sodium-ion technology has developed on a much slower timeline. The first sodium-ion energy storage system was installed in China in 2019, followed by the debut of the first sodium-ion electric vehicle in late 2023.Despite these advancements, sodium-ion accounted for less than one percent of total global production compared to lithium-ion technologies in 2025.As AI data centers strain regional power grids and extreme weather events become routine, energy operators need storage that won’t choke under heatwaves. NCO chemistry directly meets these challenges through its exceptional thermal stability and high power capability.UNIGRID’s sodium-ion technology uses a chromium-based NCO cathode chemistry. This sets it apart from other alternatives, such as sodium nickel iron manganese oxide (NFM) and sodium iron pyrophosphate (NFPP). Independent testing by the ISO-accredited Rochester Institute of Technology (RIT) Battery Development Center revealed something surprising. UNIGRID’s 210Ah cells displayed endothermic behavior during charging. This means the chemical reaction actually absorbs heat rather than dumping it into the environment.Coupled with a 97.9 percent cell-level round-trip energy efficiency and remarkable thermal stability under abuse testing, the battery stays cool on its own. The 210Ah sodium-ion cells deliver up to 218Ah of discharge capacity. It demonstrated exceptional durability, retaining over 99 percent of its capacity after 1,000 full discharge cycles, as well as heat-absorbing behavior during charging. These validated strengths allow Syntropic to optimize its product designs, enabling platforms like GridSpan to operate safely and efficiently at grid scale without needing complex mechanical cooling systems.Commercialization of the technology Further testing confirmed that NCO cells maintain exceptional thermal stability even under extreme conditions. The cells have secured the key safety and transport certifications needed to support commercial shipping and integration into full grid-scale systems.“UNIGRID’s NCO chemistry combines high round-trip efficiency, high power capability, strong cycle life performance and distinctive thermal safety behavior, providing the foundation for a GridSpan platform designed to operate without active cooling,” said Matt Huber, Chief Technology Officer of Syntropic Power.Syntropic has received its first shipment of UNIGRID NCO cells to advance its stationary energy storage portfolio. Commercialization kicks off with Tenet, a safety-focused, wall-mounted system for residential, light-commercial, and virtual power plant uses. The firm is also deploying the technology in GridSpan, its modular DC platform designed for large-scale energy applications with flexible discharge durations ranging from 20 minutes to 20 hours.Relying on abundant and widely distributed raw materials like sodium and chromium — rather than lithium and cobalt — protects manufacturers from geopolitical price spikes and material shortages.Apart from offering a alternative to lithium, a successful rollout will demonstrate a that the most durable energy storage is the kind that could stay cool entirely on its own.

title: Humanoid robots need these key technologies to work like humans
content: Building a humanoid robot is becoming more achievable as advances in AI, actuators, sensors, and battery technology make sophisticated components increasingly accessible. A new guide from the ROBO Global Robotics and Automation Index outlines the core technologies required, grouping them into three key systems: the robot’s “brain,” “body,” and “energy” source. The guide explains how AI processors, cameras, precision actuators, and next-generation solid-state batteries work together to enable human-like movement, perception, and autonomy. It also highlights the rapid growth of the humanoid robotics market, with new commercial models and supporting technologies expanding opportunities for developers, manufacturers, and investors.Humanoid robot guideAdvances in AI, robotics hardware, and battery technology are making it increasingly feasible to build humanoid robots, according to the new guide released by ROBO. The guide outlines the essential technologies needed to create a humanoid robot, describing the system in terms of three core elements: the “brain,” the “body,” and the “energy” source.The report says the biggest advantage of humanoid robots lies in their human-like form. Because they are designed with the same basic structure as people, they can navigate environments built for humans and use existing tools and equipment without requiring extensive infrastructure changes. This allows them to perform a broad range of tasks, from household chores such as loading dishwashers and organizing rooms to industrial jobs including material handling and factory assembly.To operate safely alongside people, humanoid robots require advanced perception and computing capabilities. Their “brain” combines arrays of cameras, LiDAR sensors, and tactile sensors that continuously collect information about the surrounding environment. Cameras and LiDAR generate detailed three-dimensional maps that help the robot navigate obstacles, while touch sensors in robotic hands enable it to adjust grip strength when handling objects ranging from heavy cookware to delicate glassware.Processing this vast amount of sensor data requires powerful onboard computing. Specialized AI processors analyze information in real time, allowing the robot to recognize objects, plan movements, maintain balance, and respond quickly to changes in its surroundings. These chips effectively serve as the robot’s central nervous system, coordinating perception, decision-making, and motion.Humanoid supply chainThe guide also highlights the importance of advanced actuators, which function as the robot’s muscles and joints. Modern humanoids typically combine rotary actuators for circular movements in areas such as the shoulders and hips with linear actuators that replicate the push-and-pull action of human muscles. Many robotic joints also incorporate compact, high-torque gear systems such as harmonic drives, enabling precise, stable movements while supporting heavy loads without excessive vibration.Power remains one of the biggest engineering challenges for humanoid robots. Since larger batteries increase a robot’s weight and energy consumption, manufacturers are seeking ways to improve efficiency rather than simply increasing battery size. According to the report, many next-generation humanoids are being designed to recharge autonomously or even replace their own battery packs. Developers are also exploring solid-state batteries, which promise higher energy density and improved safety by replacing flammable liquid electrolytes with solid materials.The guide notes that the commercial humanoid robotics market is expanding rapidly, with dozens of new models entering development worldwide. Alongside robot manufacturers, demand is also growing for suppliers of AI chips, sensors, actuators, precision gearing, and advanced battery technologies. As humanoids move closer to widespread deployment in homes, factories, warehouses, and service industries, the report suggests that the broader supply chain supporting these technologies is expected to play an increasingly important role in the robotics industry’s growth.

title: Boeing's 300-nautical-mile JDAM LR strike weapon enters production
content: The U.S. Air Force has cleared Boeing’s GBU-75 Joint Direct Attack Munition Long Range (JDAM LR) for initial production, marking a significant step toward fielding an affordable long-range precision weapon capable of striking targets more than 300 nautical miles (555 km) away.The Air Force awarded Boeing a $75 million Undefinitized Contract Action (UCA) for production of the BSU-111/B Payload Delivery Unit (PDU), following nearly $100 million in company-funded development. According to Boeing, the initial production will support the U.S. Navy, which has been evaluating the weapon as a low-cost stand-off strike capability.Turning a familiar bomb into a long-range strike weaponThe JDAM family has been one of the world’s most widely used precision-guided munition systems since entering service in 1999, converting conventional unguided bombs into GPS/INS-guided weapons with high accuracy. A standard JDAM typically has a range of around 15 nautical miles, while the JDAM Extended Range (ER) variant uses deployable wings to extend that to roughly 40 nautical miles.The JDAM LR pushes that concept much further. Instead of relying solely on glide, the weapon combines the familiar JDAM guidance kit, deployable wing kit, and aircraft interface with a compact turbojet engine, effectively transforming the weapon into a powered, cruise missile-like munition while retaining compatibility with existing JDAM-equipped aircraft. Boeing says the configuration enables the weapon to travel more than 300 nautical miles carrying a 500-pound (226-kilogram) payload.Designed to bridge the gap between bombs and cruise missilesOne of the JDAM LR’s biggest selling points is affordability. Rather than developing an entirely new missile, Boeing designed the weapon to leverage the existing JDAM ecosystem already used by the U.S. military and numerous allied air forces. This allows aircraft already certified to carry conventional JDAMs to integrate the long-range version with comparatively limited changes while enabling production at significantly higher volumes than many dedicated stand-off missiles.According to Boeing, the weapon is intended for precision land attack, maritime strike, and aerial mining missions, allowing aircraft to engage targets from well outside the effective range of many modern air defense systems. The company has described the JDAM LR as a system designed to supplement inventories of more expensive cruise missiles by providing a high-volume precision-strike option.Flight testing already underwayThe production decision follows a series of successful flight demonstrations conducted by the U.S. Navy earlier this year.In April, F/A-18 Super Hornets carried out two test flights over the Point Mugu Sea Range off the California coast, successfully demonstrating safe separation from the aircraft, powered flight, and precision navigation. According to the U.S. Navy, each demonstration traveled more than 200 nautical miles while maintaining guidance throughout the mission profile. Boeing later confirmed that the system has also demonstrated military-code GPS navigation and successful powered flight during testing.Why it mattersLong-range precision strike has become increasingly important as modern air-defense networks grow more capable, forcing aircraft to launch weapons from greater distances.Rather than replacing high-end cruise missiles, the GBU-75 JDAM LR is designed to complement them by offering a less expensive weapon that can be manufactured at scale while using much of the infrastructure already built around the existing JDAM family. If the program proceeds as planned, it could provide U.S. and allied forces with a significantly larger inventory of stand-off precision weapons capable of engaging land and maritime targets while keeping launch aircraft farther from contested airspace.

title: 81 years of Hiroshima bombing: Japan warns against cost of nuclear war
content: Japan has marked the 81st anniversary of the Hiroshima atomic bombing with renewed calls for a world free of nuclear weapons, as leaders and survivors warned that the lessons of 1945 remain increasingly relevant amid growing geopolitical tensions and renewed debate over nuclear deterrence.Thousands gathered at Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park on Wednesday morning to commemorate the world’s first wartime use of an atomic weapon. Representatives from more than 120 countries and regions joined survivors, government officials, and residents for the annual ceremony, where a minute of silence was observed at 8:15 a.m., the exact time the US B-29 bomber Enola Gay dropped the uranium bomb Little Boy over the city on August 6, 1945.An updated register containing the names of 353,639 atomic bomb victims was placed inside the park’s cenotaph, as Japan once again remembered those who lost their lives while urging the international community not to forget the devastating humanitarian consequences of nuclear war.Remembering the human costThe bombing destroyed much of Hiroshima within seconds. By the end of 1945, an estimated 140,000 people had died from the blast, severe burns, and radiation exposure. Three days later, the Fat Man plutonium bomb devastated Nagasaki before Japan announced its surrender on August 15, bringing World War II to a close.For many survivors, however, the suffering continued long after the war ended. Thousands of hibakusha, survivors of the atomic bombings, spent decades living with cancers, chronic illnesses, and other long-term effects linked to radiation exposure. They also became some of the world’s most prominent advocates for nuclear disarmament. According to Japanese government figures cited during this year’s ceremony, around 91,000 hibakusha remain alive today, with an average age of 86, underscoring the urgency of preserving their testimonies as the generation that witnessed the bombings continues to diminish.A message aimed at today’s worldThis year’s commemoration came against the backdrop of rising international tensions and renewed debate over nuclear deterrence.In his annual Peace Declaration, Hiroshima Mayor Kazumi Matsui warned that attempts to justify nuclear weapons as instruments of security risk repeating the tragedies of the past. “Downplaying the inhumanity of nuclear weapons and accepting the use of force to pursue one’s own prosperity risk cycles of violent retaliation that could ultimately result in another Hiroshima or Nagasaki,” Matsui said.He argued that too many political leaders continue to view nuclear deterrence as a realistic security strategy, a mindset he said pushes the goal of a world free of nuclear weapons further out of reach. Matsui also urged younger generations to learn from history and take an active role in promoting peace.Nuclear policy remains under scrutinyPrime Minister Sanae Takaichi also addressed the ceremony, emphasizing Japan’s commitment to its long-standing non-nuclear principles while renewing calls for global nuclear disarmament.At the same time, Japan’s nuclear policy remains the subject of domestic debate. Takaichi has previously expressed support for reviewing the country’s Three Non-Nuclear Principles, including the provision that prohibits the introduction of nuclear weapons into Japan. While she said Japan has upheld those principles since World War II, she stopped short of explicitly committing to maintain the current policy indefinitely.The discussion comes as concerns over nuclear security have intensified worldwide, with arms-control agreements weakening and several major powers continuing to modernize their nuclear arsenals.A warning that still resonatesMore than eight decades after the bombing, Hiroshima’s annual memorial continues to serve as both a tribute to those who lost their lives and a reminder of the consequences of nuclear conflict.As the number of living hibakusha steadily declines, the responsibility for preserving their experiences increasingly shifts to future generations. The ceremony’s message remains as relevant today as it was decades ago: while technology, politics, and global alliances may change, the humanitarian consequences of nuclear war remain unchanged—and should never be forgotten.

title: New humanoid adapts to human movement to reduce workplace injuries
content: Researchers in Italy and the UK have developed a humanoid robot that can adapt to a human partner during shared lifting tasks, helping reduce physical strain and improve workplace safety. The robot, called ergoCub, was created by scientists at GenerativeBionics, the Italian Institute of Technology (IIT), and the University of Manchester using a new human-aware design framework. The research combines robot hardware and control systems to enable safer, more adaptive human-robot collaboration. The team says the approach allows robots to interpret human movements in real time and provide ergonomic assistance during physically demanding tasks.Smarter collaborative humanoidsThe new design framework strives to transform how humanoid robots collaborate with people. Instead of treating a robot’s body as fixed hardware controlled solely by software, the team developed a system that simultaneously optimizes a robot’s physical structure and its intelligence, enabling more natural and ergonomic human-robot teamwork. The research introduces a humanoid robot called ergoCub, designed specifically to reduce the physical strain experienced by humans during cooperative lifting and carrying tasks, reports TechXplore.ergoCub uses sensors and AI to assist human lifting, reduce strain, and improve walking performance.The core technological innovation lies in what the researchers describe as shared embodied intelligence. Conventional humanoid robots are typically designed in two separate stages: engineers first finalize the robot’s hardware, then develop software to compensate for any mechanical limitations. The new framework abandons this sequential process, instead designing the robot’s body, sensors, actuators, and control algorithms together while explicitly modeling the human partner as part of the system, according to the team’s research paper.The design process begins with optimizing the robot’s morphology, including limb lengths, joint placement, weight distribution, and overall body structure. Rather than maximizing robot performance alone, these parameters are selected to improve the combined performance of the human-robot team.Once the physical design is established, the researchers develop an intelligent whole-body control architecture. The robot continuously builds and updates an internal model of its human partner using sensor data. This allows it to predict human movements, synchronize its actions, adapt to people with different body sizes and strengths, and monitor biomechanical indicators such as lower-back loading in real time.Robots learn ergonomicsThe resulting humanoid, ergoCub, is based on IIT’s iCub robot but incorporates optimized hardware and software developed using this integrated framework. During collaborative lifting experiments, the robot successfully followed human movements while dynamically adjusting its assistance according to the person’s posture and motion.A key technological capability is the robot’s ability to estimate the torque acting on a person’s lumbosacral joint—the region of the lower back most vulnerable to strain during lifting. By adjusting its own force and movement, ergoCub significantly reduced the estimated biomechanical load compared with a person performing the same lifting task without robotic assistance, reports TechXplore.The optimization process also improved the robot itself. Compared with its predecessor, ergoCub demonstrated faster walking speeds and more energy-efficient locomotion, showing that integrating hardware and intelligence benefits both collaborative and standalone robot performance.The framework treats hardware as an active contributor to intelligence rather than simply a platform executing software instructions. Sensors, actuators, mechanical design, and control algorithms operate as an integrated system that continuously adapts to both the environment and the human partner.The researchers have already extended this design philosophy to Gene.01, a next-generation humanoid developed by GenerativeBionics. Unlike one-size-fits-all humanoids, the team envisions a modular platform that can be customized for industries such as manufacturing, logistics, shipbuilding, inspection, and healthcare by adapting its sensing systems, AI models, exterior design, and end effectors to specific applications.The researchers believe this human-aware design strategy represents a significant step toward future humanoid robots that not only work alongside people but actively improve workplace safety, reduce physical fatigue, and make collaborative tasks faster, more efficient, and ergonomically safer.

title: China's new tech can plan mass strikes to hit hundreds of targets
content: China is integrating artificial intelligence into its military operations with the introduction of an AI-powered system designed to assist in planning and coordinating large-scale air strike missions, according to a report.The technology has been developed to support military commanders during complex exercises involving numerous aircraft, targets, and weapons, allowing them to prepare battle plans more quickly and efficiently, as per the report. The system reflects China’s broader strategy of incorporating advanced digital technologies into modern warfare.Newly developed AI platform functions as a decision-support toolThe newly developed AI platform functions as a decision-support tool rather than an autonomous weapon. It processes large volumes of battlefield information, evaluates mission objectives, and recommends coordinated attack plans based on available aircraft, weapon systems, and operational constraints. By automating time-consuming planning tasks, the system enables commanders to respond more rapidly to changing battlefield conditions while maintaining human oversight over critical decisions.AI could assist decision-making by calculating battlefield developments in real time, assigning the most suitable targets to different weapons and determining when munitions should be used, according to the report.Ability to coordinate simultaneous attacks on hundreds of targetsOne of the system’s primary strengths is its ability to coordinate simultaneous attacks on hundreds of targets. Modern air operations often require multiple aircraft to strike different objectives at precisely coordinated times while avoiding conflicts in airspace and ensuring efficient use of resources. The AI can rapidly calculate flight routes, assign targets, recommend weapon allocation, and adjust operational plans if new intelligence or unexpected threats emerge during a mission. This capability can significantly reduce planning time compared with traditional manual methods.The development highlights the increasing role of artificial intelligence in military command and control. Around the world, armed forces are exploring AI applications for intelligence analysis, logistics, surveillance, battlefield management, and mission planning. AI systems are particularly valuable because they can process vast amounts of information in seconds, identify patterns that may not be immediately obvious to human analysts, and generate multiple operational options for commanders to evaluate.Despite these advantages, military experts emphasize that AI should complement rather than replace human decision-making. Combat environments are highly dynamic, and unexpected developments often require judgment, experience, and ethical considerations that current AI systems cannot fully replicate. Human commanders remain responsible for approving operational plans and making final decisions, especially in situations involving significant strategic or humanitarian consequences.China’s investment in AI-based military technologies reflects a broader global trend in defence modernization. Major military powers are increasingly focusing on intelligent command systems, autonomous platforms, and data-driven decision support to improve operational effectiveness. As advances in artificial intelligence continue, future military operations are expected to rely more heavily on AI-assisted planning while maintaining meaningful human control over the use of force.The introduction of this AI-assisted air strike planning system demonstrates how emerging technologies are reshaping military strategy. By combining rapid data analysis with human expertise, such systems have the potential to improve coordination, enhance operational efficiency, and support more informed decision-making in increasingly complex combat environments.

title: US' defense innovations to get boost as top lab set to advance quantum tech
content: Quantum computing company IonQ has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Sandia National Laboratories to accelerate the co-design of quantum technologies for U.S. national security applications. The collaboration aims to combine the strengths of government research and commercial innovation to develop next-generation quantum computing and networking systems. Advancing key areas of quantum technologies for national securityThe partnership will focus on advancing key areas of quantum information science, including system optimization, device development, characterization, testing, and the integration of hardware with mission-specific applications. Research activities will be carried out at Sandia’s Quantum Demonstration Facility in New Mexico, a hub established to foster public-private collaboration and validate emerging quantum technologies for government use. According to IonQ Chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi, major technological breakthroughs often emerge when industry and government collaborate closely. He emphasized that the partnership has the potential to shape the future of quantum technology while strengthening both economic competitiveness and national security. The agreement also builds on a longstanding relationship between the two organizations. Sandia previously fabricated the ion traps used in IonQ’s earliest quantum computers. Under the new collaboration, the scope expands significantly by bringing together IonQ’s hardware and application teams with Sandia’s expertise in trapped-ion fabrication and silicon photonics. Integrated approach is expected to improve scalability of quantum computersThis integrated approach is expected to improve the scalability of quantum computers and enhance their ability to communicate through quantum networks. Sandia National Laboratories Associate Laboratories Director for Deterrence, Science and Energy, Toby Townsend, said that the collaboration reflects the laboratory’s commitment to advancing quantum technologies that will support future national security and economic competitiveness. He noted that combining the capabilities of both organizations will help accelerate innovation and translate advanced research into practical solutions for critical government missions. The partnership also expands IonQ’s presence in New Mexico, reinforcing the state’s growing quantum technology ecosystem. The Quantum Demonstration Facility provides independent validation of technologies that could pave the way toward utility-scale quantum computers, helping government stakeholders assess the readiness of emerging quantum systems. IonQ has continued to strengthen its position in the quantum computing industry through advances in trapped-ion technology. The company reported achieving a record 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity in 2025 and recently introduced its latest quantum system, IonQ Tempo. IonQ says its quantum platforms are being used across computing, networking, sensing, and cybersecurity applications, with customers including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA. As governments around the world increase investments in quantum technologies, the IonQ–Sandia collaboration highlights the growing importance of public-private partnerships in accelerating research and preparing quantum systems for real-world defense and security applications. By combining scientific expertise with commercial innovation, the initiative aims to help advance the next generation of secure, scalable quantum technologies for the United States.

title: Meta's Muse Spark 1.2 makes 1,000+ tool calls in 24-hour coding test
content:
The system can also coordinate multiple persistent background agents during a session. Instead of creating a new helper for every individual task, these agents remain active, carry out follow-up work and decide when to send information back to the main agent.
Meta says this approach is intended to reduce repeated information gathering, latency and the amount of user intervention required for multi-step engineering work.
Coding tasks that run longer
One of the more demanding tests involved GPU kernel optimization. Muse Spark 1.2 worked inside Muse Code to write, compile, profile and repeatedly improve GPU kernels over more than 1,000 tool calls, with individual runs lasting up to 24 hours.
Releasing Muse Code in beta today. It's a terminal coding agent that takes on complete software engineering tasks across large repos: planning changes, writing code, validating the results. Powered by Muse Spark 1.2, a coding-focused model update.
