title: Sequoia Capital Goes All Out on AI Under New Leaders
content: In 2023, Gavin Uberti, Robert Wachen and Chris Zhu, the co-founders of AI chip startup Etched, were still Harvard University students living in a dorm room. That was when Uberti first met with partners from Sequoia Capital. The venture firm was among the first Etched pitched that year when raising a seed round that was trying to compete in the notoriously difficult semiconductor industry. Sequoia didn’t invest then. Recently, the Menlo Park, Calif., venture firm got another chance to invest in Etched at its Series C. Before and during the fundraising round, Sequoia mounted an all-out charm offensive. Wachen hopped on a plane with Sequoia co-leader Pat Grady—who runs the firm alongside Alfred Lin—former senior Sequoia leader Doug Leone and partner Sonya Huang. The Etched cofounder also visited the Los Angeles home of another Sequoia partner, Shaun Maguire. Lin then traveled with a delegation of partners to Etched’s San Jose, Calif., headquarters to look at its chip designs. “These folks know it’s going to be a fast round, so they bring the entire partnership,” said Uberti. “It was 10-plus of the partners there. We’re in this tiny conference room.” Last month, Sequoia announced it would lead Etched’s $300 million Series C, which valued the startup at $10.3 billion. The pursuit of Etched reflects a broader shift underway inside Sequoia, a storied venture capital firm known for its early investments in everyone from Atari, Oracle and Apple to Google, Stripe and Airbnb over more than a half century. The consensus among the firm’s new leaders: AI is a bigger moneymaking opportunity than any of the big tech shifts Sequoia has seen before. Under Lin and Grady, who took over as Sequoia’s co-stewards—the term the firm uses for its co-CEOs—when Roelof Botha stepped down in November, the firm has become markedly more aggressive in pursuing AI investments after it skipped multiple opportunities to boost an early stake in OpenAI. It also opted not to invest in Anthropic at a far lower valuation than its current one. It has begun chasing AI deals at valuations it once would have considered too rich, and it is flooding the zone with its top partners to win over founders. PitchBook, which tracks the VC industry, noted in a report earlier this year that Sequoia was among the VC megafirms that had “materially accelerated” its pace of investing in early-stage companies. The change marks a sharp departure from Botha’s tenure atop Sequoia, defined in part by his more valuation-conscious approach to the AI boom, one born from the aftermath of the dot-com era’s excesses. “I see echoes of 1999. I see echoes of what happened in 2008. I see some echoes of what happened in 2021—happening now,” Botha said on a podcast weeks before his exit from Sequoia. The changes are a sign of the times. AI has scrambled the math of startup investing. Investors have begun valuing a growing number of AI companies at tens—or even hundreds—of billions of dollars within a few years of their formation. A wave of buccaneering startup investors like Thrive Capital and Menlo Ventures hasn’t hesitated to pull the trigger on eye-popping AI investments and has emerged with big paper gains as a result. Whether those markups become real returns or end up providing evidence that the old rules still apply is the question now dividing Silicon Valley. That has put leaders of firms like Sequoia on notice that they, too, must move aggressively or be left behind. One rival venture capitalist, who was among more than 20 investors, portfolio companies and others close to Sequoia interviewed for this article, observed that the “tone” of his counterparts at Sequoia has been: “We need to rebuild being No. 1.” Sequoia did not make Lin or Grady available for an interview. A person familiar with Sequoia’s investing philosophy said that Sequoia has not changed its strategy amid a time of rising valuations, but says it uses the “full force of the partnership to close deals.” Indeed, some of Sequoia’s recent funds have delivered mixed returns—especially those started at previous market peaks. As of May, the Sequoia Capital Fund, a high-profile fund launched by the firm in late 2021, had generated a 7.09% internal rate of return since the University of Texas/Texas A&M Investment Management Co. started to invest in April 2022, according to records from Utimco, a limited partner in several Sequoia funds. That figure meant the fund—which holds stakes in public companies such as Klarna, DoorDash, Block, Airbnb, Tesla and Figma as well as private companies—underperformed the S&P 500 over that period. (The documents from Utimco, obtained through an open records request, don’t specify whether its internal rate of return figures exclude Sequoia’s fees for managing the fund.) Of the three other Sequoia funds included in Utimco’s returns, the strongest performer was an $800 million venture fund launched in early 2020, which reported a 36.41% IRR from when Utimco invested later that year through this May. Meanwhile, a nearly $1.7 billion Sequoia growth fund launched in 2020 and a $195 million seed-stage fund launched in 2021 both underperformed the S&P 500 dating from when Utimco invested a few months after each fund’s launch. These funds represent only a subset of Sequoia’s portfolio. Perhaps the clearest example of Sequoia’s new posture came in February, when the firm invested in Anthropic at a $380 billion post-money valuation. Three months later, Sequoia wrote a check for more than $2 billion to co-lead Anthropic’s highly competitive Series H funding. The round raised $65 billion for the AI startup at a $965 billion valuation, including the investment, and is expected to be Anthropic’s final fundraising ahead of its planned initial public offering in the fall. The May fundraising round came together in less than a month and was highly competitive, as investors including Greenoaks jumped into the ring and the price of the potential round jumped, according to people familiar with the negotiations. Lin had a connection to the firm though. Years earlier, the AI startup’s chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, had rubbed elbows with Lin at Airbnb, where Rao was global head of corporate and business development and Lin served on the board. (In the end, Sequoia, Greenoaks, Altimeter Capital and Dragoneer Investment Group co-led the massive fundraising. No firm landed a board seat.) The Anthropic deal is one of around 20 AI-related investments the firm has announced since November. Others include another very late-stage investment in Alphabet’s robotaxi company, Waymo (Sequoia co-led the round at a $126 billion valuation). It also backed the $1.1 billion seed round of Ineffable Intelligence, a London-based AI lab founded by former Google DeepMind researcher David Silver. That round, which valued the less than one-year-old startup at $5.1 billion, marked the largest seed round in European history, according to data from PitchBook. And earlier this week, Sequoia announced that it was leading a $1 billion funding round for Valar Atomics, a nuclear power startup that hopes to deliver electricity to energy-hungry AI data centers. The funding came after another full court press from Sequoia. In early July, a delegation of the firm’s partners—including Grady and Shaun Maguire—turned up in the remote desert city of Orangeville, Utah, to see Valar generate power from its test reactor for the first time, Isaiah Taylor, Valar’s founder and CEO, said on X . Grady and Lin, who have each spent more than 15 years at Sequoia, have emphasized that as the firm’s leaders, they see their key role as bringing in deal flow. “One of the main things we want to do with Sequoia is to get it back to what it’s been for most of our 53-year-old history, where Alfred and I are doing minimal amounts of administrative work and mostly in the field making investments,” Grady told Benchmark General Partner Jack Altman on a December episode of Altman’s podcast. When he took over leadership of Sequoia in 2022, Botha’s investment approach seemed rooted in an earlier era of tech investing. Known for his early bets on YouTube and Instagram, he was skeptical of the enormous valuations commanded by AI model builders like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to three people familiar with his thinking. In 2024, Sequoia sat out investing in an OpenAI share sale led by Thrive that valued the AI startup at $86 billion and another Thrive-led round that valued it at $157 billion, in part because it was also investing in a rival, Elon Musk’s xAI. (Sequoia invested in subsequent SoftBank-led megarounds that valued OpenAI at $300 billion and $852 billion.) Instead, Sequoia took early positions in a number of AI unicorns, including Safe Superintelligence, Clay, Harvey and Sierra. Still, as revenue from the two largest AI companies surged—representing the lion’s share of all AI startups’ sales—the firm’s earlier restraint started to look misplaced. “Obviously, top AI companies scaled up very, very quickly,” said Ilya Strebulaev, a professor of finance at Stanford University’s Graduate School of Business who closely studies the venture industry. “Sequoia kind of missed out on those investments.” Strebulaev recently completed a study of the paper and cash returns of leading venture capital firms over a roughly three-decade period. Sequoia still ranked first overall, driven largely by blockbuster investments made before the AI boom, including DoorDash, Snowflake, Airbnb and SpaceX. Lin is vocal about the fact that the goalposts in venture are fast changing. “What is exceptional performance is a moving target,” he said during a February talk at the Upfront Summit, an invite-only gathering for the tech world held in Los Angeles. Case in point: Making the wall of top investments in Sequoia’s office once required a $100 million gain. It now involves earning upward of $1 billion. “I’m sure in a few years we’ll be looking at $10 billion or more,” he added. To the outside world, Botha’s departure in November as Sequoia’s top leader seemed sudden and extraordinary for a firm that has had only a small handful of leaders over its 54-year history. Sequoia offered little explanation about the leadership change beyond publishing a note written by Botha describing it as the latest in the firm’s tradition of passing leadership “from one generation to the next.” In Lin’s case, there wasn’t much of a generational change: He’s one year older than Botha. Inside the firm, though, tensions built up in the years leading up to Botha’s departure. His first year as the firm’s global leader, 2022, was defined by a brutal market downturn due to rising interest rates that rattled Sequoia on multiple fronts. The company took a particularly nasty black eye when it was forced to write off its $200 million investment in embattled crypto exchange FTX. The Sequoia Capital Fund, in particular, became a source of frustration for some of Sequoia’s limited partners , which include many university endowments and nonprofits. Sequoia set up the fund in October 2021 to hold stock in companies after their IPOs. Soon after, public markets tumbled. Sequoia later eased rules around the fund, allowing limited partners to extract some capital earlier. A person familiar with the firm’s investing said it is “evolving some of the fund mechanics to allow for greater flexibility.” There were broader concerns around Botha’s leadership. One person who worked with Botha described him as a top-down leader whose style clashed with the firm’s traditionally collaborative partnership. Meanwhile, two people described a chilly relationship between Botha and Sequoia’s limited partners. The person who worked with Botha also highlighted his personal investing track record, arguing that he lacked recent wins like those of Leone, who led Sequoia’s investments in Wiz and Nubank while he was steward. Botha’s defenders point to his deep operating and board experiences, including longtime director roles at Block, Unity, Natera and MongoDB, as well as a CFO role at PayPal, as giving the firm credibility with entrepreneurs. He also handed board positions to younger partners and often helped them win deals, a former investor said. And by the ultimate measure of how limited partners judge VC firms—actual cash distributions—Botha’s tenure leading the U.S. business between 2017 and 2025 was a record-breaking period for the firm. The CEO of one Sequoia-backed company that counts Botha as a longtime board member pointed to the VC firm’s current roster of investors as a testament to his leadership. “He has absolutely recruited and developed the best team in venture,” said the CEO, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. As for complaints about his leadership style, they said they’ve only had positive interactions with Botha, whom they described as “just a great investor and board member.” One of the final challenges of Botha’s stewardship came last July after Shaun Maguire, the partner behind the firm’s investment in SpaceX, drew backlash after posting since-deleted comments on X in which he called Zohran Mamdani, then a mayoral candidate in New York, an “Islamist” who “comes from a culture that lies about everything.” Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire during the Hill & Valley forum at the US Capitol in Washington, D.C, in April 2025. Photo by Al Drago/Getty Images Things finally came to a head when Lin, Grady and Andrew Reed, three of Sequoia’s most senior partners, met with Botha to discuss his time at the firm. The firm exercised an undisclosed “mechanism” to choose its leadership, said a person familiar with the process. Botha ultimately agreed to step down while keeping his existing board seats at Block, Unity and other companies. In an announcement made November 4, he said he would continue to serve as a Sequoia adviser. Botha still maintains close connections to powerful figures in tech. In June, he was appointed to the board of SpaceX, whose founder and CEO, Elon Musk, worked with Botha at PayPal. No current Sequoia partner serves on SpaceX’s board, despite Sequoia’s sizable investment in the company. Around the same time, Botha’s bio was scrubbed from the Sequoia website. About a month later, he announced on LinkedIn that he had “concluded my transition from Sequoia Capital.” Sequoia’s new guard comes with strong reputations among founders. Lin in particular is a known entity in Silicon Valley. He joined Sequoia in 2010 after helping build and sell Zappos, the Sequoia-backed online shoe retailer he co-founded with the late Tony Hsieh. Over the next 16 years, Lin became one of Sequoia’s most prolific and influential investors, helping lead the firm’s investments in DoorDash, Uber and Citadel Securities and representing it on the board of companies like Airbnb. According to Strebulaev, the Stanford University professor, DoorDash has generated the biggest returns of any investment in Sequoia’s history. Founders describe Lin as a workhorse—regularly responding to emails, texts and calls after midnight and as early as 4 a.m.—with deep expertise in startup operations and finance. “He’s very, very good at looking behind corners, because he’s seen so much,” said Kalshi founder Tarek Mansour. Kalshi, which Sequoia backed during its 2021 Series A, is one of Sequoia’s big recent wins. As a Kalshi board member, Lin’s involvement extends to sometimes interviewing job candidates for the prediction markets startup. He also frequently serves as a sounding board for key decisions in which he’ll “always take the opposite side in any argument,” Mansour said. “He has a bit of a Socratic method.” “Most investors are nice to your face and toxic when you’re not in the room,” said Keller Rinaudo Cliffton, co-founder of Zipline, a drone-delivery unicorn Sequoia invested in back in 2012 (Lin is on the company’s board). “Alfred is the opposite: often mean in the room and unwaveringly supportive outside it.” Sarah Guo, founder of Conviction, right, and Pat Grady, partner at Sequoia Capital, during the Allen & Co. Media and Technology Conference in Sun Valley in July. Photo by David Paul Morris/Getty Images Grady joined Sequoia at age 24 after spending nearly three years at Summit Partners, a Boston-based investment firm. Now 43 and a decade younger than Lin, he’s considered greener than his counterpart, according to two investors who know him. Despite that, he led the firm’s lucrative investment in Snowflake and other firms. More recently, he’s gotten the firm into buzzy AI companies including drug research startup Chai Discovery, legal software platform Harvey and medical search engine OpenEvidence. One venture capitalist who knows Grady described him as having a “win-at-all-costs mentality.” His longtime friend Bill Clerico, founder of Convective Capital, said Grady is someone who likes to “push himself to the extreme” in all parts of his life. He’ll run the Dipsea Trail, a grueling route more than seven miles long that covers rolling hills and gains 2,000-plus feet in elevation in Marin County, and then do it again, Clerico said. Despite Grady’s intensity, Christopher O’Donnell, founder of Day AI, an AI-native customer relationship management platform backed by Sequoia, described him as measured and understated. O’Donnell was chief product officer at HubSpot when he first met Grady, then a HubSpot board member. Based on Grady’s reputation, O’Donnell expected someone decades older to walk into the room. Instead, O’Donnell recalled, “I meet him and he’s this very friendly, kind of stoic, very fit, late 20s guy.” After learning about Botha’s departure, Havi Nguyen, founder of Abby Care, a healthcare startup backed by Sequoia, texted Lin, who sits on Abby Care’s board, to congratulate him. Lin’s response to her was brief. “The job has never changed,” Nguyen said Lin told her. The message from Lin and Grady is clear: They’re not going to disappear into the administrative duties of running the firm. Rather, they plan to remain active investors. Since taking over as co-steward, Lin has led at least four deals announced by the firm, including its investment in Ineffable Intelligence; Rowspace, an AI platform for financial services firms; and Firetiger, a startup building tools to check code written by agents. One big question is whether they can maintain that pace while balancing the broader responsibilities of running Sequoia. Lin and Grady collectively sit on 21 company boards and continue to advise dozens of startups as investors. They are also now responsible for shaping the firm’s strategy and managing relationships with limited partners. “Everybody congratulated me and Pat from the outside,” Lin told “Sourcery,” a tech industry podcast, in a March interview. “And then everyone on the inside was like, ‘My condolences to you—you have to deal with all of us.’” Sequoia Capital’s Alfred Lin (left) and Collaborative Robotics CEO Brad Porter speak during the HumanX AI Conference 2025 in Las Vegas. Photo by Big Event Media/Getty Images So far, founders say they have not noticed a difference in Lin and Grady’s availability or engagement, according to conversations with five portfolio company leaders. “I really think he’s even more responsive,” said Kareem Amin, co-founder and CEO of Clay, which counts Lin as a board member. “We’re making a lot of strategic decisions, so I feel like I’m spending more time with him.” Max Rhodes, co-founder and CEO of online marketplace Faire, recalled seeing Lin at Maria Isabel, a Mexican restaurant near the Presidio in San Francisco, on a recent Friday evening. While waiting for his wife, Lin had his laptop open and had turned a restaurant table into a workspace. “He was just there grinding,” said Rhodes. The breadth of the workload may help explain why Lin and Grady bought back Leone in March as Sequoia’s chair. “When we realized how much gas Doug has left in the tank, we invited him to ramp up as an investor at Sequoia,” Grady posted on X when announcing his return on March 31. One source close to the firm had a different take, suggesting Leone is back to “babysit” Lin and Grady. “Why are three people required to replace one?” this person asked. A person familiar described this characterization of Leone’s role as “inaccurate” and said that Grady and Lin wanted him back on the investing team. Still, one Silicon Valley leader who saw Grady at the Sun Valley Conference hosted by Allen & Co. in July described the Sequoia leader as appearing “much more fluid” and “happy” than he had in previous encounters. He was “firing on all cylinders,” the person said. Sequoia’s new leadership was also on display at the firm’s annual Base Camp retreat in late June. The multiday event included a laser tag match alongside Sequoia partners, camping under the stars and an off-the-record conversation between Lin and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over glasses of whiskey. (Sequoia wrote the first check in Nvidia.) For more than a decade, Sequoia has used Base Camp to convene many of Silicon Valley’s most influential founders and executives; past speakers include Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. The event is a reminder of the firm’s enduring influence, which, as one San Francisco investor pointed out, it would take a lot to erode. “It would probably take a decade of poor performance and scandal to kill Sequoia,” said the venture capitalist, who previously worked in the investment office of a university endowment that invested with the firm. “Do you want to be known as the person who said no to Sequoia and then their next fund had a trillion-dollar company?”

title: A Meta AI Model Hacked Another Company During Cybersecurity Testing
content: A Meta Platforms artificial intelligence model accessed the internet during cybersecurity testing and hacked into another company, according to people familiar with the matter, in the latest in a string of such incidents at major AI firms. Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 model breached the systems of a company and made changes to its internal systems, said one of the people, who said the AI was able to access the public internet because of an error in the set up of the “sandbox” testing environment. Meta worked on that testing with an outside evaluation partner called Irregular, the people said. A Meta spokesperson said Irregular caused the misconfiguration and the model subsequently exploited a security vulnerability in another third-party service “in a manner similar to previously-reported instances with other companies.” Meta learned of the incident when Irregular notified it, and “we are currently investigating and will issue a full retrospective once we have all the facts,” the Meta  spokesperson said. A spokesperson for Irregular said the Meta incident didn’t involve a sophisticated cyber action by the models and that there are “no current open issues.” The spokesperson said Irregular is developing a white paper outlining best practices for containment and the secure execution of cyber evaluations. Similar episodes disclosed by OpenAI and Anthropic in recent weeks have fueled concern about the security implications of advanced AI. Anthropic last week said a review of its systems had found its AI models also exploited access to the internet during cybersecurity tests. The models reached the internet because of a configuration mistake in the test environment that also was managed by Irregular, and the models subsequently accessed the systems of three organizations, said Anthropic. The spokesperson for Irregular said on Wednesday that the Meta incident involved “the exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week.” The Anthropic disclosure came after OpenAI said last month that its models broke out of the company’s systems during cybersecurity testing and hacked model repository Hugging Face. The ChatGPT-maker had instructed its AI agent to solve a particular software vulnerability in what was supposed to be an isolated sandbox, but the model figured out how to access the internet and break into Hugging Face’s systems to find the answers to the test. OpenAI and Anthropic said they were taking measures to strengthen testing practices. On Tuesday, the UK AI Security Institute published a report detailing incidents in which Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol AI models took actions against people and organisations. In one case, the AISI said, an AI agent used social engineering—tactics to manipulate humans to divulge sensitive information—in an attempt to get malicious code approved for an open-source project. The AI agent created fake online identities and used them to pressure the project’s maintainer into approving the code. The incidents reported by AISI occurred during cybersecurity tests in which the models were given internet access, but they highlight the lengths to which AI agents may go in pursuing their assigned goals. Even before the recent incidents, U.S. government officials were growing increasingly concerned about the cybersecurity implications of powerful new AI models. The Trump administration issued an executive order in June on establishing voluntary testing for new frontier AI models, and on Tuesday administration officials briefed companies on a new framework for implementing that order. People in the AI industry have also called for better safety protocols. Last month, more than 1,100 senior executives and employees at companies including Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google signed an open letter calling on governments to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

title: Apollo Taps New AI Sector Head to Chase More Megafinancings
content: Apollo Global Management is looking to turn its blockbuster $35 billion Broadcom financing deal into repeat business, naming a new leader to coordinate teams and land more financing business from chipmakers and other tech companies at the center of the AI build-out. The firm in recent months tapped partner Reed Rayman to lead its chip-focused coverage, one piece of a broader strategy to source more digital infrastructure deals and connect them with investment teams across Apollo, two people familiar with the move said. Rayman’s role will focus on developing relationships to help Apollo lead more big, complex AI infrastructure financings, one of the people said. Apollo and other big asset managers are trying to position themselves to capture more business from the large-scale financing needed to continue the AI infrastructure build-out. Some high-profile projects are too large for traditional corporate loans, spawning a web of partnerships, backstops and other arrangements to spread the risk among AI labs, chip and cloud firms, and lenders. While Apollo is best known for investing clients’ money in private equity, credit and other funds it manages, it also has a capital solutions business that earns fees by assembling large deals and pulling in other investors and lenders. The firm still makes most of its money from managing investments and its insurance business, but arranging deals is a growing source of revenue, helping offset the weak profits it’s seen recently from selling its private equity investments. The financing Apollo arranged for Broadcom earlier this year will help Google deploy its custom AI chips with Anthropic as the customer using the compute capacity. In that deal, a special purpose vehicle will buy Google’s chips, which it developed with Broadcom, and lease them to Anthropic. Broadcom provided a backstop for the bulk of that debt. Apollo as well as rival Blackstone will keep some of the debt in funds they manage and sell the rest to other investors and lenders. The development of the data centers the chips will go in is financed separately from the $35 billion chip deal, including through setups where Google backstops the lease payments in a way that allows the developers to issue cheaper debt. Apollo already has a broad team working on AI-specific deals, with about 60 people focused on digital infrastructure, one of the people said. Rayman is specifically focused on sourcing lending deals backed by semiconductors and their lease payments, the person said, as opposed to financing other aspects of AI infrastructure such as data centers, power or real estate. Apollo oversees large pools of insurance capital , including through its Athene arm. Financing backed by leases of chips, such as Google’s tensor processing units and Nvidia’s dominant AI chips, can be attractive to insurers. Insurers typically invest premiums in long-term debt with predictable payments so they can make payouts to policyholders down the line. The deals that finance chips use the hardware as collateral and often feature corporate guarantees to ensure the end user pays its lease. Those protections help the debt secure investment-grade ratings while still offering higher yields than similarly rated corporate bonds. Rayman describes the role on his partner profile page as “overseeing the firm’s global coverage of the AI and digital infrastructure ecosystem as part of a cross-firm effort to bring Apollo’s full range of capital solutions to leading technology companies.” It couldn’t be learned when exactly he took on the new AI role. He reports to Chris Edson, Apollo’s global head of origination, the person said, who oversees finding, underwriting and funding new loans and investments. Rayman also reports to Jamshid Ehsani, who leads Apollo’s global principal structured finance business. Ehsani’s team arranges and invests in big loans backed by assets or contracts—such as data center or aircraft leases—across sectors. The new role for Rayman builds on recent moves by Apollo to expand its work on large financings for capital-intensive businesses. In December, Apollo separated its hybrid business from its traditional private equity business, making it into a stand-alone unit overseen by partner Matt Nord with Rayman as deputy co-head, the Financial Times reported . The hybrid business makes big investments combining debt and equity. Ahead of Apollo formalizing the hybrid unit as a stand-alone business, Rayman helped launch a multibillion-dollar partnership with Joe Lonsdale’s venture firm, 8VC, to identify tech companies with capital-intensive projects seeking larger financings than typical venture rounds. Before moving into hybrid investing, Rayman focused on private equity deals and led the firm’s $5 billion buyout in 2021 of Verizon’s media business, which included Yahoo and AOL. Blackstone has taken its own cross-team approach to some of its AI investing. The firm announced in April that Jas Khaira would lead a newly created group called Blackstone N1, which inherited Blackstone’s growth equity business and coordinates AI investments across other parts of the firm. Khaira, who also heads the tactical opportunities strategy in the Americas, led Blackstone’s early financing of CoreWeave. ‘Unprecedented’ Buildout Apollo has already been active in financing chips or related assets. In 2024, Apollo led an $11 billion investment to acquire a 49% stake in an Intel semiconductor manufacturing facility in Ireland. Earlier this year, it helped pair a $3.5 billion financing with a $1.9 billion Nvidia commitment to enable a unit of Valor Equity Partners to buy chips and lease them to xAI. The firm has been active in other areas of AI  infrastructure besides chip-focused deals. Apollo majority-owns Stream Data Centers alongside minority owner and insurer Principal Financial Group, and recently bought a European colocation business from Blue Owl–owned Stack Infrastructure, though its exposure to data center assets is smaller than some rivals’. Apollo President Jim Zelter highlighted the opportunity for the company to play a growing role in the AI build-out on the firm’s second-quarter earnings call Tuesday. “The sheer size of the AI infrastructure build-out is unprecedented,” Zelter said. “We see ourselves playing a critical role in partnering with the leading firms and providing these flexible scaled solutions to support their needs.” Across all industries, Apollo’s capital solutions business has originated more than $130 billion across 190 transactions, largely over the last two years. Apollo said its fees from arranging and financing deals jumped 28% from the year-ago period, to a record $277 million, more than a third of the firm’s total fee-related earnings. That’s not yet reflecting fees from the Broadcom deal, which Apollo expects to recognize as the funds are drawn, mostly later this year and in the first three quarters of 2027. Apollo’s assets under management meanwhile climbed to $1.05 trillion as of the end of the second quarter, though realized performance fees dropped 41% as the firm held off on some private equity exits.

title: Clarity Act Won’t Be Enough to Bring Crypto Boom Back
content: After helping elect President Trump in 2024, the crypto industry had high hopes for getting legislation providing a clear regulatory framework for the sector—which the industry hoped would unlock a huge wave of new interest from big money and mainstream investors alike. That bill, known as the Clarity Act, is now looking unlikely to pass this year. And given uncertainty about who will control Congress after this year’s midterms, crypto companies have to confront the unwelcome reality that they’ve missed their best shot to gain permanent legitimacy in the eyes of regulators. If the Clarity Act doesn’t pass before the mid-terms, it may not pass under a Democrat-controlled House or Senate. That’s a long-term problem for crypto. Regulators have been friendly to crypto under Trump, but the industry remains exposed to crackdowns under future administrations. Yet that lack of regulatory protection isn’t actually the industry’s biggest problem right now.  Even if the Clarity Act passes, it would provide far less of a business boost to crypto than many had originally assumed. That’s because crypto is deep in another bear market. Bitcoin has fallen to pre-2024 election levels and is down by half from its October peak. And while the industry has been through these kinds of crypto winters before, this one appears likely to have a lasting impact. Take last month’s announcement by two long-running exchanges—BitMEX, co-founded by bitcoin evangelist Arthur Hayes, and Bitmart—that they were shutting down. BitMEX said it decided to close after a strategic review of the business and the broader crypto industry, and Bitmart cited operating conditions and the market environment for its plan to wind down. Meanwhile, there are signs that individual investor interest has moved from betting on crypto to real world wagers. Robinhood, for instance, reported last week that prediction market revenue surpassed crypto trading revenue for the first time in the second quarter. There’s no obvious reason why investors’ interest in real world wagers will reverse—even if the Clarity Act passed. In fact, prediction markets tend to pick up around big event cycles like elections, so we’ll see what the fall holds. New forms of crypto hacks also keep popping up, hurting crypto’s standing even with diehard fans. Last week, hackers stole more than $100 million worth of Bitcoin from thousands of addresses on physical hardware wallets made by Canada-based Coinkite. That shocked the Bitcoin holders who have long believed cold storage was the safest way to protect their wealth. Security breaches are nothing new, of course, and memories have typically been short. Hackers stole a record $1.5 billion from Bybit last year, while this year, the largest decentralized lending platform, Aave, suffered from a run after hackers deposited bad collateral. But with crypto prices showing no sign of shaking their slump and breaches coming from unexpected corners, investors may see less of a risk-reward tradeoff for holding crypto. There’s also not much argument for an acceleration in institutional adoption of crypto, which has typically been a catalyst for price gains in the past. Banks have been moving into blockchain technology, to be sure, but much of that focuses on stablecoins and putting traditional financial assets on-chain. They have less interest in moving into more speculative crypto markets. Even if the Clarity Act passes, it’s unclear how much additional appetite that will unlock from traditional banks, especially while markets remain weak. “I don’t think the banks particularly care about the crypto parts of it. There’s just not that much interest in crypto per se these days,” said Joe Cox, partner at Oliver Wyman who advises banks and a former regulator at the Federal Reserve. Cox said where banks are focused is in stablecoins, deposit tokens, and building capital markets on-chain. Wells Fargo, this week, announced it will offer its deposits on the blockchain for corporate and commercial clients to move money across borders this fall. The Genius Act has already provided legal certainty for stablecoins, so those bank priorities are much less tied to the outcome of the Clarity Act. And as we wrote a few weeks ago, Coinbase and JPMorgan’s partnership to tie crypto deeper into consumer banking—via features like converting credit card reward points into crypto—is delayed. The two firms, meanwhile, have been facing off over stablecoin-related aspects of legislation. Even if they get over their differences, it’s tough to see how much urgency a big bank will have in rolling out consumer features while crypto is in a slump. Meanwhile, some of the fastest-growing corners of crypto—such as perpetual futures on offshore venue Hyperliquid—are not covered by the Clarity Act at all, so even the bill’s passage won’t immediately help encourage regulatory risk-averse banks to lean in to capture a hot market. “The pathway for Hyperliquid to be accessible to U.S. users does run through the agencies, not through Congress,” said Jake Chervinsky, CEO of Hyperliquid Policy Center, which advocates for Hyperliquid.

Wie verändern neue Radwege, Fahrradstraßen oder Verkehrsberuhigungen den Radverkehr in einer Kommune? Welche Infrastrukturmaßnahmen werden von Radfahrenden angenommen und führen dazu, dass Menschen gern mit dem Fahrrad unterwegs sind? Antworten auf diese Fragen liefert RadSim, eine neue Webplattform der Technischen Universität Dresden (TUD), die ab sofort Kommunen bei der datenbasierten Radverkehrsplanung unterstützt.
Die im Rahmen des Forschungsprojekts „Radverkehrssimulation zur Verbesserung der kommunalen Radverkehrsplanung (RadSim)“ entwickelte Anwendung simuliert auf Basis wissenschaftlicher Modelle, wie sich Veränderungen im Verkehrsnetz auf die Wahl der Routen und die Verteilung der Radverkehrsströme auswirken. Kommunen können so verschiedene Szenarien simulieren, unkompliziert miteinander vergleichen und deren Auswirkungen auf den Radverkehr virtuell erproben, bevor sie umgesetzt werden. Dadurch lassen sich Planungsprozesse fundierter gestalten und Investitionsentscheidungen auf eine belastbare Datengrundlage stützen.
„Mit RadSim stellen wir erstmals ein wissenschaftliches Werkzeug bereit, mit dem sich unterschiedliche Planungsvarianten bereits vor ihrer Umsetzung realitätsnah simulieren lassen. Das schafft eine fundierte Entscheidungsgrundlage und hilft dabei, öffentliche Mittel dort einzusetzen, wo sie den größten Nutzen für den Radverkehr und die Menschen vor Ort haben“, so Projektleiter Dr.-Ing. Stefan Huber.
Wissenschaftliche Modelle auf Basis realer Routendaten
Grundlage der Simulationen sind wissenschaftlich entwickelte Modelle des Routenwahlverhaltens von Radfahrenden. Diese wurden an der Professur für Verkehrsökologie aus anonymisierten Bewegungsdaten der STADTRADELN-App entwickelt und in die Webanwendung integriert.
Die Modelle ermöglichen unter anderem Aussagen darüber, welche Maßnahmen besonders attraktiv für Radfahrende sind, wie sich Radverkehrsströme innerhalb einer Kommune durch Maßnahmen verlagern, welche Netzabschnitte stärker oder weniger genutzt werden und wie unterschiedliche Planungsvarianten im direkten Vergleich wirken.
Mehr Lebensqualität durch bessere Radverkehrsplanung
Von den Erkenntnissen profitieren nicht nur kommunale Planungsämter. Eine zielgerichtete Radverkehrsplanung schafft langfristig sicherere, komfortablere und besser vernetzte Radverkehrsangebote. Das kann mehr Menschen motivieren, Alltagswege mit dem Fahrrad zurückzulegen und trägt gleichzeitig zu weniger Verkehrslärm, geringeren Emissionen und einer höheren Aufenthaltsqualität im öffentlichen Raum bei.
Mit RadSim stellt die TUD Kommunen damit ein wissenschaftlich fundiertes Werkzeug zur Verfügung, das datenbasierte Entscheidungen erleichtert und einen wichtigen Beitrag zu einer nachhaltigen und zukunftsfähigen Mobilitätsplanung leistet.
Das Forschungsprojekt „Radverkehrssimulation zur Verbesserung der kommunalen Radverkehrsplanung (RadSim)" wird vom Bundesministerium für Verkehr (BMV) aus Mitteln zur Umsetzung des Nationalen Radverkehrsplans gefördert. Das Gesamtvolumen beträgt 621.456,74 Euro.
Die Plattform steht teilnehmenden Kommunen der Kampagne STADTRADELN mit einer ausreichenden Datengrundlage kostenfrei zur Verfügung.

title: Sind Gasturbinen bereit für die Wasserstoffwirtschaft?
content:
Sind Gasturbinen bereit für die Wasserstoffwirtschaft?
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Das Bildmaterial darf nur in Zusammenhang mit dem Inhalt dieser Pressemitteilung verwendet werden. Xizhen Dong untersuchte wie sich Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt. Solche Legierungen werden unter anderem für Turbinenschaufeln in Gasturbinen und Flugzeugen eingesetzt.
| Copyright:
Max-Planck-Institut für Nachhaltige Materialien GmbH
Download
Internationales Forschungsteam zeigt, wie Wasserstoff Turbinenwerkstoffe bei hohen Temperaturen schädigt.
Auf den Punkt gebracht:
• Herausforderung: Gasturbinen für die Stromerzeugung und Luftfahrt werden bislang mit fossilen Brennstoffen betrieben und verursachen 15% der weltweiten Kohlendioxid-Emissionen. Wasserstoff gilt als CO2-freie Alternative. Bislang war unklar, wie sich Wasserstoff bei hohen Temperaturen auf die Turbinenschaufeln aus Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt.
• Forschungsfrage: Was geschieht mit Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen, wenn sie bei hohen Temperaturen Wasserstoff ausgesetzt werden?
• Ergebnisse: Wasserstoff versprödet den Turbinenwerkstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen mindestens doppelt so schnell wie bei Raumtemperatur. Verursacht wird die Versprödung durch chemische Reaktionen zwischen Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff, die Karbide abbauen und Methan bilden. Dies führt zu frühem Materialversagen.
• Ausblick: Karbide erhöhen die Festigkeit von Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen. Gleichzeitig greift der Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen genau dort an. Um Gasturbinen mit Wasserstoff zu betreiben, müssen künftige Legierungen auf andere Festigungsmechanismen zurückgreifen.
Gasturbinen, die mit fossilen Brennstoffen betrieben werden, liefern 22% des globalen Stroms. Gleichzeitig sind sie für 15% der weltweiten CO2-Emissionen verantwortlich. Um Gasturbinen CO2-frei zu betreiben, könnte Wasserstoff als umweltfreundliche Alternative in Gasturbinen zur Stromerzeugung und in der Luftfahrt eingesetzt werden. Doch wie beeinflusst Wasserstoff Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen – der Werkstoff aus dem die Turbinenschaufeln bestehen – unter den extremen Bedingungen innerhalb der Turbine?
Während die Wirkung von Wasserstoff auf metallische Werkstoffe bei Raumtemperatur bereits intensiv untersucht wurde, ist über das Verhalten bei erhöhten Temperaturen wie in Gasturbinen, bislang deutlich weniger bekannt. Ein internationales Forschungsteam unter anderem vom Max-Planck-Institut für Nachhaltige Materialien (MPI-SusMat) hat untersucht, wie sich Wasserstoff bei erhöhten Temperaturen auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen auswirkt. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass die Turbinenschaufeln bei erhöhten Temperaturen mindestens doppelt so schnell verspröden wie bei Raumtemperatur. Dies stellt eine erhebliche Herausforderung für Bauteile dar, die höchsten Anforderungen an Sicherheit und Zuverlässigkeit genügen müssen.
Die Forschungsergebnisse wurden jetzt in der Fachzeitschrift Nature Materials veröffentlicht.
Warum Wasserstoff bei hohen Temperaturen schädlicher ist
„Dringt Wasserstoff bei Raumtemperatur in eine Nickelbasis-Superlegierung ein, setzt er sich in der Regel an Grenzflächen und Versetzungen fest und führt zur Versprödung. Bei erhöhten Temperaturen kommt noch ein weiterer Effekt hinzu: Wasserstoff dringt in die Karbide, die eigentlich für die Festigkeit des Werkstoffs verantwortlich sind, und verbindet sich dort mit Kohlenstoff. Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff reagieren zu Methan, welches einen hohen lokalen Druck auf die Grenzflächen zwischen Karbiden und Nickelmatrix ausübt und so schneller zu Materialversagen führt“, erklärt Dr. Xizhen Dong, Postdoktorandin am MPI-SusMat und eine der Erstautorinnen der Studie.
Die Temperatur ist entscheidend
Dong und ihr Team untersuchten, wie sich Wasserstoff auf Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen bei Temperaturen zwischen 400°C und 1000°C auswirkt. Mithilfe der Atomsonde analysierten sie den Werkstoff auf atomarer Ebene und simulierten die Bildung von Methan mit Methoden der Dichtefunktionaltheorie. Dabei konnten sie zeigen, dass wasserstoffbedingte Schädigungen aufgrund thermodynamischer Bedingungen ausschließlich bei 400°C auftreten. Denn nur bei dieser Temperatur ist die Reaktion von Wasserstoff und Kohlenstoff zu Methan thermodynamisch begünstigt. Oberhalb von 400 °C wurde keine Methanbildung beobachtet.
„Dieses Ergebnis ist insbesondere für Gasturbinen in der Energieerzeugung und für Flugtriebwerke von großer Bedeutung“, erklärt Professor Dierk Raabe, Direktor am MPI-SusMat und einer der korrespondierenden Autoren der Studie. „Im Gegensatz zu stationären Dampfturbinen, die dauerhaft bei sehr hohen Temperaturen laufen, werden Gasturbinen häufig an- und abgeschaltet. Dadurch sind sie einem deutlich größeren Temperatur- und Belastungsspektrum ausgesetzt und genau in diesem Bereich kann wasserstoffbedingte Versprödung verstärkt auftreten.“
Zwischen hoher Festigkeit und Wasserstoffresistenz
Karbide erhöhen die Festigkeit von Nickelbasis-Superlegierungen, Stählen und Verbundwerkstoffen. Die jetzigen Untersuchungen zeigen allerdings, dass bei erhöhten Temperaturen und der Verwendung von Wasserstoff als Energieträger Karbide die Eintrittspforte für Wasserstoffversprödung sein können. Um zukünftig Gasturbinen mit Wasserstoff und somit CO2-frei betreiben zu können, sollten alternative Verfestigungsmechanismen gefunden werden. Alternativ müssten die Werkstoffe so angepasst werden, dass ein ausgewogenes Verhältnis zwischen der durch Karbide erzielten Festigkeit und der Widerstandsfähigkeit gegenüber wasserstoffinduzierter Versprödung erzielt wird.
Die Ergebnisse unterstreichen, wie wichtig es ist vorhandene Legierungen unter realen Einsatzbedingungen zu testen, um deren Sicherheit und Lebensdauer optimieren zu können.
Die Studie wurde von Forschenden der East China University of Science and Technology (China), des Max-Planck-Instituts für Nachhaltige Materialien (Deutschland) und der Hunan University (China) geleitet.

title: Fraunhofer startet techHAUS: Digitalisierung für Unternehmen einfach gemacht
content:
Fraunhofer startet techHAUS: Digitalisierung für Unternehmen einfach gemacht
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Das Bildmaterial darf nur in Zusammenhang mit dem Inhalt dieser Pressemitteilung verwendet werden. Falls Sie das Bild in höherer Auflösung benötigen oder Rückfragen zur Weiterverwendung haben, wenden Sie sich bitte direkt an die Pressestelle, die es veröffentlicht hat.
techHAUS: Digitalisierung. Einfach. Machen.
| Copyright:
© Fraunhofer FIT
Download
Mit dem neuen Projekt techHAUS macht Fraunhofer FIT Digitalisierung für Unternehmen konkret erlebbar. Vor allem kleine und mittlere Betriebe im Rheinischen Revier können hier KI, Extended Reality, Web3 und Automatisierung kennenlernen, testen und den Mehrwert für das eigene Geschäftsmodell einschätzen. Ziel ist es, Orientierung zu geben, Fehlinvestitionen zu vermeiden und Innovationen schneller in die Praxis zu bringen. Das Angebot: Workshops, Demonstratoren, Prototypen und Weiterbildung. techHAUS ist ab sofort für Unternehmen, Kommunen und Interessierte geöffnet.
Viele kleine und mittlere Unternehmen möchten Künstliche Intelligenz, Extended Reality, Automatisierung oder andere digitale Technologien nutzen. Im Tagesgeschäft fehlen jedoch oft Zeit, Ressourcen und Orientierung, um die richtigen Technologien auszuwählen und sie sinnvoll und wirtschaftlich einzusetzen.
Hier setzt das neue Projekt techHAUS des Fraunhofer FIT an: Als gefördertes Strukturwandelprojekt im Rheinischen Revier hat techHAUS den Auftrag, digitale Technologien für Unternehmen einfach zugänglich zu machen. Es entsteht ein Ort, an dem Unternehmen Zukunftstechnologien kennenlernen, ausprobieren und ihre Potenziale für das eigene Unternehmen bewerten können. Ziel ist es, Digitalisierung greifbar zu machen, Fehlinvestitionen zu vermeiden und Unternehmen dabei zu unterstützen, Innovationen schneller in die Praxis zu bringen. Dafür bündelt techHAUS die langjährige Forschungskompetenz des Fraunhofer FIT und vermittelt praxisnah den Einsatz digitaler Technologien, darunter Web3, Extended Reality und KI.
Prof. Wolfgang Prinz, Co-Projektleiter von techHAUS und stellvertretender Leiter des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Angewandte Informationstechnik FIT, bringt das Leistungsportfolio für Unternehmen auf den Punkt: »Viele Unternehmen stehen nicht vor der Frage, ob sie digitalisieren müssen, sondern wie. Genau dabei unterstützen wir. Wir helfen Unternehmen dabei, die richtigen Technologien für ihre individuellen Herausforderungen zu finden, sie praktisch auszuprobieren und fundierte Entscheidungen für ihre nächsten Digitalisierungsschritte zu treffen.«
Das Angebot richtet sich in erster Linie an kleine und mittlere Unternehmen aller Branchen. Darüber hinaus steht techHAUS auch Kommunen, Initiativen sowie Bürgerinnen und Bürgern als Anlaufstelle für Fragen rund um digitale Technologien offen. Unternehmen bringen ihre Fragestellungen und Herausforderungen ein und erhalten Orientierung bei der Bewertung digitaler Technologien sowie Impulse für ihre eigenen Digitalisierungsvorhaben. Die daraus entstehenden Demonstratoren, Methoden und Prototypen werden öffentlich zugänglich gemacht und fördern den Wissenstransfer für Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft. Ergänzt wird das Angebot durch Weiterbildungen, Studien und Veranstaltungen, die Unternehmen dabei unterstützen, digitale Entwicklungen einzuordnen und gezielt für die eigene Zukunft zu nutzen.
Mit dem Projekt leistet techHAUS einen Beitrag zum Strukturwandel im Rheinischen Revier und stärkt die Innovationskraft der regionalen Wirtschaft. Das Projekt wird im Rahmen des STARK-Programms durch das Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördert und vom Ministerium für Wirtschaft, Industrie, Klimaschutz und Energie des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen begleitet.
Co-Projektleiterin Lisa Klug äußert sich folgendermaßen zur Rolle von techHAUS in der digitalen Transformation: »Digitalisierung darf keine zusätzliche Belastung sein. Sie muss Unternehmen dabei helfen, effizienter zu arbeiten, Fachkräfte zu entlasten und wettbewerbsfähig zu bleiben. Unser Ziel ist es, digitale Technologien verständlich, praxisnah und einfach zugänglich zu machen, damit aus Innovation konkrete Wertschöpfung entsteht.«
Interessierte Unternehmen können sich ab sofort unverbindlich über Workshops, Demonstrationen und Mitwirkungsmöglichkeiten im techHAUS informieren. Sie möchten mehr über das techHAUS und seine Angebote erfahren? Unsere Ansprechpartnerinnen und Ansprechpartner stehen Ihnen gerne zur Verfügung.
Die offizielle Eröffnung des techHAUS findet am 8. Oktober 2026 im Beisein von Mona Neubaur, Ministerin für Wirtschaft, Industrie, Klimaschutz und Energie des Landes Nordrhein-Westfalen, statt. Interessierte Unternehmen, Kommunen und Personen können sich ab sofort anmelden. Weitere Informationen und die Möglichkeit zur Anmeldung finden Sie unter
https://techhaus.de/

title: Den CO2-Fußabdruck eines Industrieprodukts einheitlich, vergleichbar und verständlich berechnen: So geht‘s
content:
Den CO2-Fußabdruck eines Industrieprodukts einheitlich, vergleichbar und verständlich berechnen: So geht‘s
Wie lässt sich der CO₂-Fußabdruck eines Produkts standardisiert, automatisiert und unternehmensübergreifend entlang der Wertschöpfungskette ermitteln? Und wie gelingt dies in Unternehmen, die dafür nur über begrenzte (Personal-)Ressourcen verfügen? »PCF Guidance«, der neue Leitfaden der Plattform Factory-X, an dem das Fraunhofer IWU mitgearbeitet hat, beschreibt Berechnungsmethoden und enthält konkrete Berechnungsbeispiele für Fertigungsprozesse wie Fräsen, Schmieden und additive Fertigung. Es erweitert den Betrachtungsraum auf die industrielle Fertigung von Produkten, die aus mehreren Teilen oder Baugruppen bestehen (diskrete Fertigung).
Der neue Factory-X-Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« ergänzt das Rulebook der Plattform Catena-X, das auf einer höheren Abstraktionsebene und mit Schwerpunkt Automobilindustrie grundlegende Berechnungsstandards setzt.
Warum den CO2-Fußabdruck erfassen? Was ist ein PCF?
Für große Unternehmen besteht bereits bzw. entsteht die Pflicht, über Klima- und Emissionsdaten zu berichten (CSRD, Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive der Europäischen Union). Dabei müssen häufig auch Emissionen aus Produkten und Lieferketten berücksichtigt werden. Noch greift die ESPR-Verordnung (Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation), die schrittweise den Digitalen Produktpass (DPP) mit umfassenden Nachhaltigkeitsdaten einführt, für den Großteil der Fertiger nicht. Doch die künftige Regulatorik führt dazu, dass viele Kunden von ihren Zulieferern bereits heute Produkt- oder Material-CO₂-Daten anfordern.
Factory X adressiert den Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) als eine zentrale Herausforderung für die diskrete Fertigung. Für einen Produkt-PCF müssen alle Beiträge zu einem durchgängigen CO₂-Fußabdruck (von der Rohstoffgewinnung bis zum Fabriktor, »Cradle-to-Gate«) aggregiert werden. Ein PCF beschreibt die einem konkreten Produkt zuzurechnenden Treibhausgasemissionen, typischerweise in kg CO₂e (CO₂-Äquivalent). Für die diskrete Fertigung bedeutet das beispielsweise, die Beiträge des Rohmaterials (Stahl, Aluminium, Kunststoff), der Transporte und vorgelagerten Lieferantenprozesse sowie den Energieverbrauch der Fertigungsanlagen und die Hilfsstoffe zu berücksichtigen – heruntergebrochen bis auf das einzelne Bauteil.
Was der Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« leistet
Ziel der Autoren ist es, den CO₂-Fußabdruck eines Produkts standardisiert und automatisiert aus Prozess-, Energie-, Material- und Logistikdaten berechenbar und über Unternehmensgrenzen hinweg nachvollziehbar zu machen. Der Leitfaden erläutert verständlich, wie Unternehmen systematisch Emissionsdaten aus Eigenfertigung und Lieferkette erfassen, zu einem Cradle-to-Gate-PCF zusammenführen und dabei Anforderungen wie Systemgrenzen oder Cut-off-Regeln (beispielsweise Grenzwerte, Stichtage oder Ausschlusskriterien) berücksichtigen.
Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der möglichst verursachungsgerechten Zuordnung von Energie- und Materialverbräuchen zu einzelnen Produkten. Dazu werden drei detaillierte Berechnungsbeispiele für ein Frästeil, ein Schmiedeteil und eine additiv gefertigte Dämpfergabel vorgestellt, inklusive Formeln, Datenquellen und der Behandlung von Ausschuss, Verpackung und Transporten.
Darüber hinaus beschreibt das Dokument, wie Emissionen in Mehrproduktfertigungen über Prozessunterteilung (»Process Subdivision«), Systemerweiterung (»System Expansion«) oder Allokation (physisch beziehungsweise wirtschaftlich) verteilt werden können. Es empfiehlt dafür die räumliche und zeitliche Prozessaufteilung durch Submetering (Einzelerfassung) und die Nutzung von Produktionsdaten, um den Anteil von Schätzungen und Zuordnungen zu reduzieren. Zusätzlich enthält der Leitfaden konkrete Praxisbeispiele zur Allokation von Gebäudeemissionen, Stillstandszeiten und Maschinenverbräuchen.
Orientierung, Hilfestellung und Angebot zur Kooperation
Der mit Beteiligung von ESTAINIUM, Siemens, dem Fraunhofer IWU und weiteren Partnern erstellte Leitfaden »PCF Guidance« (Product Carbon Footprint Guidance) entstand auf Basis des Catena‑X PCF Rulebook V4.0. Kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen bietet er eine wichtige Orientierungshilfe; das Fraunhofer IWU unterstützt gern bei der korrekten Berechnung eines PCF.
Austauschbarkeit der Daten
Über den Factory-X-Datenraum können Lieferanten und Kunden PCF-Daten standardisiert austauschen, sodass sich CO₂-Informationen entlang der gesamten Wertschöpfungskette nachvollziehen lassen. Dies schafft die Grundlage für kommende regulatorische bzw. kundenseitige Nachhaltigkeitsanforderungen.
Factory-X betrachtet dabei insbesondere den Cradle-to-Gate-Ansatz. Perspektivisch soll der Austausch von diesen Daten auch für kleine und mittlere Unternehmen auf Basis von Catena¬-X ermöglicht werden: Unternehmen behalten stets die vollständige Kontrolle über ihre Daten (Datensouveränität). Bei stark arbeitsteiligen Herstellprozessen über Unternehmensgrenzen hinweg lässt sich ein Cradle-to-Gate-Ansatz für die Ermittlung des CO2-Fußabdrucks nur im Rahmen automatisierter Prozesse und über sichere Daten-Ökosysteme effizient umsetzen.
Kurz erklärt...
DISKRETE FERTIGUNG bezeichnet die Herstellung von Produkten, die aus mehreren Teilen oder Baugruppen bestehen und meist wieder in ihre Einzelteile zerlegt werden können. Solche Produkte sind stückweise zählbar, werden aus einzelnen Komponenten montiert oder zusammengebaut und weisen oft eine hohe Variantenvielfalt auf. Ihre Fertigung basiert auf Stücklisten und Arbeitsplänen.
FACTORY-X ist ein vom Bundesministerium für Wirtschaft und Energie gefördertes Projekt, das einen offenen Datenraum für die gewerbliche Wirtschaft aufbaut. Ziel ist es, Daten zwischen Unternehmen sicher, standardisiert und souverän auszutauschen, ohne dass die beteiligten Firmen die Kontrolle über ihre Daten verlieren. Der Fokus liegt auf Anwendungsfällen wie Product Carbon Footprint (PCF), Digital Product Passport (DPP), Lieferkettentransparenz, Resilienz und Nachhaltigkeit.
CATENA-X Technisch baut Factory-X auf Konzepten aus Catena X und der Verwaltungsschale (Asset Administration Shell) auf, um Daten entlang der gesamten Wertschöpfungskette interoperabel nutzbar zu machen. Catena X ist ein offenes, kollaboratives Datenökosystem insbesondere für die Automobilindustrie.
Factory-X bzw. der Leitfaden erhalten Fördermittel des Bundesministeriums für Wirtschaft und Energie bzw. der Europäischen Union.

title: Ola Electric, Axis Energy plan to deploy up to 20 GWh of battery storage by 2032 - Energy Storage
content: Ola Electric has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with renewable energy developer Axis Energy to deploy as much as 5 GWh of BESS per year from 2028. The MoU runs until 2032 with a cumulative target of 20 GWh over the five-year period, providing Indian EV manufacturer Ola Electric with a significant pipeline for its new manufacturing platform – Ola Mahashakti . Scheduled to launch on August 15, Ola Mahashakti is being billed as an energy storage platform for commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. Ola said its Mahashakti battery energy storage systems (BESS) are being developed in India on a vertically integrated manufacturing platform spanning cell technology, manufacturing, and system engineering. The deal with Axis Energy sees Ola partner with a developer building one of India’s largest pipelines of storage-backed renewable projects. Axis Energy has secured grid approvals for over 3.75 GW projects in Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan and has another 3.5 GW capacity in pipeline. These projects, spanning firm and dispatchable renewable energy (FDRE), hybrid, and other non-solar configurations, will require large-scale BESS to improve renewable energy integration, enhance grid reliability, and deliver firm, round-the-clock clean energy. The national opportunity for BESS is even greater. The Central Electricity Authority has said India’s energy transition will require 400+ GWh storage deployment by 2032. Reddy Kataru, chairman and managing director of Axis Energy Ventures, described the MoU with Ola as an “important step” toward evaluating domestic BESS solutions. Bhavish Aggarwal, chairman and managing director of Ola Electric, said that the company’s vertically integrated cell-to-system platform will enable it to deliver a strong proposition across safety, performance and total cost of ownership. “Axis Energy is our first large-scale partner and an important early validation of Mahashakti’s potential. We are witnessing a strong interest from potential partners in the industry, and this MoU further strengthens our momentum in building long-term partnerships,” Aggarwal said. Headquartered in Hyderabad, Axis Energy Ventures has more than 15 years of experience in developing and delivering renewable energy projects across India. The company has more than 1.5 GW of commissioned capacity and a development pipeline of over 8.5 GW. Axis Energy Ventures has a strategic partnership with Brookfield Renewable through Evren, a 51:49 joint venture backed by Brookfield’s $20 billion Global Transition Fund II. Ola Electric Mobility’s Ola Future factory in Tamil Nadu produces electric vehicles and components. It is supported by Ola’s Bengaluru-based Battery Innovation Centre (BIC), dedicated to advancing cell and battery technology. title: Serentica Renewables commissions first phase of 1 GWh Bikaner battery project - Energy Storage
content: Serentica Renewables has commissioned the first phase of its 1 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in Bikaner, Rajasthan. The project represents the first time the renewable energy arm of Vedanta Group has delivered a large-scale BESS for the commercial and industrial segment. The first phase of the project comprises a 50 MW/200 MWh BESS. The Bikaner BESS has been developed with a modular architecture to provide operational flexibility, scalability and rapid response capabilities. Serentica Renewables said its Bikaner project powers one of the world’s first time-block round-the-clock (RTC) renewable power arrangements for industrial consumers, demonstrating how battery storage can transform intermittent renewable energy into dependable, 24/7 clean power. “Battery energy storage systems will play a defining role in the next phase of India’s clean energy transition by making renewable energy available whenever it is needed,” said Akshay Hiranandani, CEO, Serentica Renewables. “The commissioning of phase 1 of our 1 GWh BESS is a significant milestone in our journey to deliver reliable, round the clock renewable energy for India’s industrial sector. By integrating advanced storage with renewable generation, we are creating a future ready energy ecosystem that combines sustainability, reliability and flexibility for our customers.” Established in 2022, Serentica Renewables is an independent power producer (IPP) with 3.2 GW of renewable energy capacity. The IPP has ongoing projects across multiple states, leveraging a mix of solar, wind, energy storage, and advanced balancing solutions. These include a planned 7 GWh battery order pipeline for the next two years. The post Serentica Renewables commissions first phase of 1 GWh Bikaner battery project appeared first on Energy Storage .

title: CATL-backed CNTE brings Czech Republic’s largest battery online - Energy Storage
content: The Czech Republic’s largest completed BESS project is now online, serving the European frequency regulation market. Located on a former mining wasteland, the 37.95 MW/41.7 MWh Modlany BESS features 11 liquid-cooled, 20-foot energy storage containers supplied by CNTE. CNTE is invested by Chinese battery giant CATL, and its STAR T-285 containers supplied to the Modlany project use CATL’s lithium-ion phosphate cells. Each container is rated at 3.45 MW/3.793 MWh and supports 1P charging and discharging and is suitable for one-to-four-hour systems, according to CNTE. The Modlany project, which also includes 42.7 MW of solar, is connected to a high-voltage substation and provides grid balancing and fast-response frequency regulation services. The battery can store excess solar power and can rapidly charge or discharge depending on grid requirements, helping to balance electricity demand and fluctuations in solar generation throughout the Czech electricity system as it adds more renewables. Modlany’s owners Katemo Group state on their website that the planned storage capacity is “up to 130 MWh”. The Czech engineering company is working with CATL and CNTE to bring BESS to the Czech and Slovak markets and it has kitted its Modlany battery out with its own energy management software designed to optimize performance and adhere to cybersecurity standards. The future of the Czech Republic’s energy storage market will be driven by utility-scale investments and favorable regulations, according to analysis by Aurora Energy Research from November 2025. The agency forecasted the country’s total battery storage capacity to hit 6 GWh by the end of the decade. In March 2025, the European Union approved an aid package for 1.5 GWh of storage capacity in the Czech Republic. Other battery players besides CNTE are watching the growing market closely. China’s AlphaESS signed agreements in December 2025 to deliver a combined 320 MWh of BESS across two sites in the Czech Republic, which when completed will eclipse Modlany’s capacity. Headquartered in Fujian Province, China, CNTE is active in the C&I and residential segments as well as smart electric vehicle charging. In the utility-scale market, it has projects in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Austria, and China. It is also present in South Africa, Uganda and other European markets through its C&I activities. title: Ørsted turns on 500 MWh battery project with co-located solar in Texas - Energy Storage
content: The 250 MW/ 500MWh  Old 300 Storage project in Needville, Texas, has reached commercial operations according Ørsted, co-located with a 430 MW solar project. Old 300 Storage is fully integrated into the ERCOT grid and will be operated independently from the Old 300 Solar installation, which has been generating since 2024. Energy storage for the project comprises Tesla Megapacks manufactured at the company’s Lathrop, California facility. Ørsted said the developer and Tesla have been working in collaboration with the Needville Fire Department to provide “comprehensive education” on the energy storage technology and safety response protocols. Melissa Peterson, president of Ørsted Americas Onshore noted that BESS has been playing a larger role on the ERCOT grid, providing power at times of tight supply and demand margins. “Achieving commercial operations at our Old 300 Storage project will have tangible benefits, such as strengthening grid reliability by providing additional resources to Texas grid operators and allowing for more diverse and localized energy options as electricity demand continues to grow.” Old 300 Storage is part of a growing onshore portfolio developed by Ørsted in the United States. Major projects include a 300MW/1200MWh BESS located developed with Salt River Project and located alongside the Eleven Mile Solar Center in Pinal County, Arizona. The project was commissioned in 2024 and represented an approximate $1 billion investment by Ørsted in clean energy for Arizona Following the Old 300 BESS entering commercial operations, Ørsted now has a 6 GW of operational onshore US energy projects. The international developer, which has its global headquarters in Denmark, estimates the Old 300 solar and storage projects combined will inject approximately $110 million in property tax revenue for the local area. title: US grants $490 million loan for 220 MW of battery capacity in Puerto Rico - Energy Storage
content: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has closed a $489.4 million loan with Dawn Puerto Rico, a subsidiary of Pattern Energy, to fund 220 MW of battery energy storage systems in Puerto Rico. The facility will be located in Arecibo and Santa Isabel and will use battery technology made in the United States, according to the DOE’s Energy Domain Financing Office. The agency did not specify the energy capacity of the systems, expressed in MWh, or their duration of discharge. The DOE estimates that batteries will be able to provide backup electricity to more than 100,000 customers during periods of supply shortages. It also estimates that it will prevent approximately 13 million cumulative hours of service interruptions, taking as a reference the network operational data for 2025. The loan would reduce the electricity costs of Puerto Rican households and businesses by about $312.5 million over the next 25 years, according to US government projections. The funding was restructured following a review by the current US administration. In addition to the two battery projects, the agreement provides for a way for the possible future development of dispatchable electricity generation powered by natural gas. The DOE did not report the power, location or timetable of that eventual infrastructure. The closed operation changes the scope of the conditional commitment announced by the DOE in January 2025. That proposal included three independent BESS systems with a joint power of 180 MW and a capacity of 720 MWh, in addition to a 70 MWac photovoltaic plant with integrated storage. The new announcement raises total storage power to 220 MW, but no longer includes photovoltaic installations. Nor does it detail how the power is distributed between the projects of Arecibo and Santa Isabel. Since 2025, the DOE has issued several emergency orders under section 202(c) of the Federal Energy Act to authorize generation and other actions aimed at maintaining Puerto Rico’s electricity supply during periods of high demand and during hurricane season. title: Growatt brings MINA to all-in-one home storage - Energy Storage
content: Growatt has launched MINA, a single-phase all-in-one residential energy storage system combining a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, backup power and intelligent energy management. The company is targeting rooftop solar markets in Europe and Australia, where time-of-use tariffs, lower solar export payments and rising electricity prices are increasing demand for household self-consumption and energy resilience. MINA is available with inverter output ranging from 3 kW to 10 kW. Its battery can be configured with one to six 5 kWh modules, providing total usable storage capacity of between 5 kWh and 30 kWh. The system supports three maximum power point trackers, with one string connected to each tracker, and a maximum DC-to-AC ratio of 2.0. Maximum input current is 18 A per tracker, allowing the inverter to accommodate newer high-current PV modules. Growatt said its battery optimizer technology manages each module independently. This is designed to reduce the effect of differences in state of charge, operating history or ageing between battery modules. It also allows homeowners to add new modules to an existing system as household demand increases. Potential expansion scenarios include the addition of electric vehicles, heat pumps, home offices or higher backup requirements. The architecture enables customers to install a smaller system initially rather than paying for the maximum capacity at the time of commissioning. MINA provides a 63 A backup connection and can supply selected household loads during grid outages. A preliminary European datasheet lists a transfer time of less than 10 milliseconds, intended to maintain operation of lighting, refrigeration, communications and other essential equipment with minimal interruption. The system incorporates self-aligning connectors and a wire-free stacked battery architecture. Growatt claims the hardware can be stacked in around 10 minutes, with system setup and diagnostics completed in a similar period. It can be installed on the floor or mounted against a wall. Other features include Type II surge protection on both the AC and DC sides, arc-fault protection, natural cooling and remote monitoring. Users and installers can view PV generation, battery status, household consumption and operating performance through Growatt’s monitoring platform. The system is also virtual-power-plant ready. Growatt lists a 25-kW bidirectional DC charging function for future vehicle-to-grid applications, although this feature is not yet commercially available. Growatt has already presented MINA in Australia. The latest announcement broadens its commercial positioning across Germany, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, Australia and other residential storage markets. title: Electrovaya unveils 7 MW containerized battery system targeting AI data centers - Energy Storage
content: Lithium-ion technology company Electrovaya has launched the ElvaPulse 1500, a high-power stationary battery energy storage system designed for data centers, artificial intelligence infrastructure, and mission-critical power applications. The launch marks the debut product under Electrovaya’s new ElvaPulse stationary storage portfolio, engineered specifically to handle high-surge, rapid-discharge power requirements driven by volatile AI compute workloads. Housed in a standard 20-foot modular container, the 1,500 VDC architecture delivers up to 2.88 MWh of nominal energy capacity and can supply approximately 7 MW of continuous power. The unit is built around the company’s proprietary ceramic separator technology that underpins its Infinity Battery line. The battery unit operates at a discharge duration of under 30 minutes, representing a C-rate greater than 2C. Electrovaya states this high power density allows facilities to reduce physical site footprints and cut balance-of-system costs compared to standard 2- to 4-hour utility-scale storage profiles. The platform targets microgrids, peak-demand management, industrial power quality, and renewable energy firming in addition to hyperscale data centers. Electrovaya Chief Executive Officer Raj DasGupta said the platform was purpose-built to meet pushing energy demands by offering high power density alongside proven battery longevity and configuration flexibility. Initial commercial deliveries are targeted for the second quarter of 2027 out of Electrovaya’s manufacturing facility in Jamestown, New York. Certification processes for UL 1973 and UL 9540 are currently underway with completion targeted for the first quarter of 2027, and the company is currently accepting production reservations while engaging in active discussions with hyperscale and energy developers. title: PV recycling challenges unlikely to be the same everywhere - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team of scientists from Australia and Japan has developed correlation and spatial validation models to characterize the relationships between economic, social, geographical, and climatic features and PV decommissioning dynamics, including PV waste generation and PV lifespan.
“Most studies on end-of-life solar panels focus on how much waste will be generated and when it will appear,” said corresponding author Jian Zuo to
pv magazine
. “Our research goes one step further by asking why these patterns differ across regions. Instead of only projecting future PV waste, we investigated how broader economic, social, geographical, and climatic conditions are associated with PV waste generation and PV lifespan.”
Zuo added that by combining machine learning with spatial analysis, the group provides “a new way to understand the regional context behind PV decommissioning, offering evidence that can support more informed planning for future PV recycling and product stewardship.”
The researchers developed a three-stage machine-learning framework to identify the contextual factors associated with PV decommissioning in Australia. Using data from 2,634 postcodes, they trained machine-learning algorithms to predict previously modeled PV waste generation and PV lifespan under three Australian energy market operator decarbonization scenarios: progress change (PC), step change (SC), and green energy export (GEE).
They used 15 higher-level contextual variables for their prediction, which comprised three economic indicators: household income, rent, mortgage repayments; four social indicators: population, families, household size, private dwellings; two geographical indicators: PV power output and optimum module tilt; and six climatic indicators: rainfall, temperature, direct normal irradiation, global horizontal irradiation, diffuse horizontal irradiation, and global tilted irradiation.
The research framework | Image: Adelaide University,
Environmental Impact Assessment Review, CC BY 4.0
In the first stage of the framework, five machine-learning models -XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, long short-term memory (LSTM), and support vector machines (SVM) were trained separately for PV waste generation and PV lifespan. XGBoost achieved the best performance for PV waste prediction, while LightGBM performed best for PV lifespan.
In the second stage, the researchers used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify how strongly each contextual variable contributed to the predictions and whether its influence was positive or negative. Finally, they applied multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) to test whether these SHAP-derived relationships remained statistically significant and spatially consistent across Australia.
“One of the most interesting findings was that different types of factors matter for different aspects of PV decommissioning,” said Zuo. “We found that PV waste generation is more strongly associated with socioeconomic features, such as population, families, dwellings, income, and rent; while PV lifespan is more strongly associated with geographical and climatic conditions, including rainfall, temperature, and solar irradiation.”
The researcher further explained that these relationships vary considerably across Australia, suggesting that future PV recycling challenges are unlikely to be the same everywhere. “My team is planning to conduct more studies examining the dynamic interactions among policy, economic conditions, technological advances, and stakeholder attitudes, as it is essential for understanding solar system retirement decisions,” he said.
The framework has appeared in “
Spatiotemporal correlations of PV decommissioning: Machine-learning insights from socioeconomic and geoclimatic data
,” published in
Environmental Impact Assessment Review
. Researchers from Australia’s
Adelaide University
, commercial construction company
and Japan’s
Sophia University
have contributed to the study.

The EU has greenlit a €780m ($900m) Dutch state aid scheme to support up to 400MW of green hydrogen production capacity.
The package will award funding by early 2027 through a competitive bidding process, with selected projects receiving 10-year variable per-kilogramme subsidies and direct grants covering up to 80% of investment costs.

, which encompasses hydrogen-based fuels, and its
